docs.title: JDBC
docs.text:
Ingest tables from a live PostgreSQL database — full dumps or watermark-incremental, resumable mid-table, scheduled by cron.

Type jdbc-generic Protocol JDBC (postgres) Target connector.t_<name> Schedulable cron Edition Open

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: acme-erp-pg
  connector_type: jdbc-generic
  scopes: [erp, billing]
spec:
  connection:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db.acme.io:5432/billing
    user: ro_user
    password_env: ACME_DB_PASSWORD
  source:
    tables:
      - name: invoices
        mode: watermark
        watermark_column: updated_at
        pk_columns: [invoice_id]
  target: {}

lm validate -f acme-erp-pg.yaml
lm apply -f acme-erp-pg.yaml
lm connector run acme-erp-pg

docs.title: Guided flow — lm source jdbc
docs.text:
The manifest above is one road in; lm source jdbc is the other, and it comes right after Quickstart on purpose — for a non-developer installer, the interactive road is the one to try first, with the YAML manifest reference below as what to reach for once you want repeatable, version-controlled config. The password is always read from stdin, never a flag:

printf '%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" | lm source jdbc test --url jdbc:postgresql://... --user ro_user
printf '%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" | lm source jdbc discover --url ... --user ... [--schema public] \
    [--skip-pattern 'pg_*,information_schema*,t_*'] [--include-views] [--output table|json]
printf '%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" | lm source jdbc add my-source --url ... --user ... \
    --tables invoices,customers [--template-mode llm-first|heuristic-only|dump-1-1] \
    [--schedule-cron '0 6 * * *'] [--interactive]
lm source jdbc list-tables my-source
  • test — connection check: dialect, server version, latency, visible schemas.
  • discover — lists tables with row estimates, columns, PK and a suggested watermark column.
  • add — creates one connector per table plus a mapping. --interactive opens a TUI table picker (pre-filled with the discovered watermark suggestions); otherwise pass --tables. The password is stored as an encrypted Basic credential (<source-name>--credential), created and managed by this guided flow — it never lands in a config file.
  • --template-mode picks how the mapping template is drafted: llm-first (default — the local LLM drafts it from sampled rows, falling back to the heuristic when no LLM is available or the draft is unusable), heuristic-only, or dump-1-1 (no transformation).

docs.title: Connection
docs.text:
connection:
  url: jdbc:postgresql://db.acme.io:5432/billing  # required
  user: ro_user                                    # required
  password_env: ACME_DB_PASSWORD                   # required — server env var (see below)
  dialect: postgres           # optional, inferred from url scheme; `postgresql` accepted as an alias

Supported dialects (v1): postgres. If dialect is declared and differs from the URL scheme, validation fails.

The connection user only needs SELECT on the declared tables — nothing more. Every jdbc query, whether an ingestion run, discover, or test, only ever reads: ingestion issues SELECT * FROM <schema>.<table> and discovery/introspection use the driver's read-only metadata calls. Nothing in the jdbc connector inserts, updates, deletes or alters anything on the source database.

docs.title: Password sources
docs.text:
At run time the password is resolved in priority order:

Priority Source Notes 1 Attached credential A Basic credential referenced by the connector (connector.credential_id), stored encrypted. The guided lm source jdbc add flow creates one automatically (named <source-name>--credential); manifests applied via lm apply don't set this. 2 password in config Plain-text fallback, dev/test only. 3 password_env The name of a variable in the hub server's environment (an OS env var, or a JVM system property). Unset at run time = a clear run failure. If you don't operate the hub yourself, ask whoever does to export it where the hub runs. Unlike the CSV transports' key_env/password_env, this does not consult the lm secret registry — the value must exist in the server environment.

"Stored encrypted" means pgcrypto AES-256 under LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY — the key, its no-rotation posture and its caveats live in Security → Secrets at rest.

Never put a real password in a manifest

Priority 2, plain password in config, is a dev/test fallback only.

docs.title: Source — multi-table
docs.text:
Each entry in source.tables[] becomes an endpoint of the connector — one runnable unit per table (you'll see them in the TUI). The endpoint name = table name; the endpoint path = /<table-name>. Two modes: watermark — incremental, tracked via a column that only grows on change (e.g. updated_at) — or full — a complete, PK-ordered re-scan.

source:
  tables:
    - name: invoices
      mode: watermark               # watermark | full
      watermark_column: updated_at  # required when mode=watermark
      pk_columns: [invoice_id]      # required, non-empty
      # any source column sharing a reserved hub-column name needs `rename:` (see the warning below)
      indexes:                      # optional — Postgres indexes on the hub table
        - { columns: [customer_id], unique: false }
    - name: customers
      mode: full
      pk_columns: [customer_id]

Seven column names are reserved on jdbc's hub tables

id, _row_hash, _ingested_at, _source, _run_id, _mapping_version, tenant_id — the hub adds these to every table jdbc-generic, csv-file and kafka create (they all write through the same connector.t_<name> machinery; REST/GraphQL/SOAP land in a differently-shaped table with its own reserved names — see REST). A source column sharing one of the seven is refused at write time, naming the column and the fix — on a brand-new table and on one that already exists alike, so a later run never silently drops that column's values. id is the one you'll hit most (an ERP's own primary key almost always uses it), but it isn't special — any of the seven collide the same way. See Target for the fix.

docs.title: Deletes at the source are never propagated
docs.text: A row deleted at the source stays in the hub table — in both modes, forever, since neither watermark nor PK-cursor reads ever notice an absence. To resync from scratch, delete and re-create the connector: lm connector delete purges its connector.t_* tables (and its RAG chunks), so the next apply + run starts clean.

docs.title: Per-table indexes
docs.text: Declarative indexes are per-table for jdbc (that is where the runtime reads them — spec.target.indexes is not read by this connector type, unlike CSV & files, where target.indexes at the connector level is exactly what's read). Each entry is { columns: [non-empty strings], unique?: bool } (unique defaults to false); malformed entries fail validation with a per-entry error instead of being silently dropped.

docs.title: Watermark resume — composite cursor
docs.text:
If a run is interrupted, the next one resumes exactly where it left off — no duplicates, no gaps.

mode: watermark — the cursor is composite: {col: <watermark_column>, value: <last watermark>, pk: {<first pk column>: <last value>}}. Resume reads WHERE col > value OR (col = value AND pk > last_pk) — ties in the watermark column paginate stably via the first pk_columns entry as tiebreak. Scheduled runs are incremental for free: the persisted cursor carries the last watermark forward, so only rows changed since then are re-read.

mode: full — the cursor is PK-only (pk > last_pk), so full scans are chunked and resumable. It captures inserts by ascending PK but, having no watermark, never re-reads updated rows.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
defaults provides per-table fallbacks. Each tables[i] field overrides the corresponding default. Shallow merge (no recursive merging).

defaults:
  schema: public
source:
  tables:
    - name: invoices
      mode: watermark
      watermark_column: updated_at
      pk_columns: [invoice_id]
      # schema inherited from defaults
    - name: line_items
      schema: billing               # overrides defaults.schema for this table only
      mode: watermark
      watermark_column: ts
      pk_columns: [invoice_id, line_no]

Chunking is fixed, not a knob

Reads page through the source in 500-row chunks (keyset pagination on the primary key, so a full scan of millions of rows stays linear and memory-bounded). There is no chunk_size setting — a manifest that declares one is refused at validation rather than silently ignored, the same refuse-rather-than-ignore rule as the CSV parser's fixed chunking.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
schedule — optional cron expression for the connector as a whole. All tables ingest on the same trigger. The hub scheduler evaluates cron times in UTC, not the server's local timezone — write your expression accordingly.

If the source is a sensitive production database, schedule ingestion off-hours to keep its read load away from business-hours traffic — see Sizing & load tests.

docs.title: Target
docs.text:
The métier scope is not a target concern — it is declared on the connector, as metadata.scopes (see Scopes); the connector warns at validate-time when none is declared. What lands under target is about the hub table itself.

Tables are created in the connector schema as connector.t_<name> (one per declared source table). A source column sharing one of the seven reserved names above (see the warning under Source; id is the one you'll hit most) is refused.

Fix it with rename: — a per-table map from the source column name to the hub column name you want instead, declared right beside pk_columns:

source:
  tables:
    - name: invoices
      pk_columns: [invoice_id]
      rename:
        id: source_id       # source column `id` lands in the hub table as `source_id`

rename: is an ordinary per-table key, so it can also live under defaults: when every table needs the same rename (see Defaults above). A table's own rename: replaces the one from defaults: entirely rather than merging with it — defaults: is a flat, per-key overlay, so declaring rename: on a table means that table's rename: is exactly what you wrote there, nothing inherited.

The rename only changes the column name in the hub table — nothing is renamed, altered, or written back on the source database, so the connection stays read-only. lm validate's refusal rules for rename: are in Validation rules below.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text: Rule Severity Path connection.url matches jdbc:<dialect>:... ERROR spec.connection.url Dialect in supported set (postgres) ERROR spec.connection.url Declared dialect matches URL scheme ERROR spec.connection.dialect source.tables[] non-empty ERROR spec.source.tables Each tables[i].mode in ERROR spec.source.tables[i].mode mode=watermark requires watermark_column ERROR spec.source.tables[i].watermark_column pk_columns is a non-empty list ERROR spec.source.tables[i].pk_columns chunk_size is refused — not a knob, chunking is fixed at 500 ERROR spec.source.tables[i].chunk_size indexes entries are { columns: [non-empty strings], unique?: bool } ERROR spec.source.tables[i].indexes[j] No duplicate table names ERROR spec.source.tables[i].name rename target is a plain identifier ERROR spec.source.tables[i].rename rename target is not one of the seven reserved names ERROR spec.source.tables[i].rename No two rename sources target the same column ERROR spec.source.tables[i].rename schedule (if present) is a valid cron ERROR spec.schedule window (if present) is HH:MM-HH:MM ERROR spec.window metadata.scopes declared WARNING metadata.scopes

docs.title: Keep ingestion out of the source's business hours
docs.text:
The DBA's condition for the SELECT account is usually a clock, not a row count. Declare it:

spec:
  schedule: "*/30 * * * *"
  window: "22:00-06:00"    # UTC — the scheduler's clock

Result: cron slots due outside the window are skipped, never queued — with the pair above, the source is read every 30 minutes between 22:00 and 06:00 UTC and left alone the rest of the day. Windows may cross midnight (that is the point). Three edges to know: the end is exclusive — a cron slot landing exactly on the end time is skipped, so a nightly 0 6 * * * needs a window ending 06:01 or later (22:00-07:00); a manual lm connector run bypasses the window — it is an explicit operator act; and re-applying a manifest without window lifts the fence (same column-is-truth contract as schedule).

docs.title: Discover tables and pick interactively
docs.text:
printf '%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" | lm source jdbc discover --url jdbc:postgresql://db.acme.io:5432/billing --user ro_user
printf '%s\n' "$DB_PASSWORD" | lm source jdbc add my-source --url jdbc:postgresql://db.acme.io:5432/billing --user ro_user --interactive

Result: discover lists tables with row estimates and a suggested watermark column; add --interactive opens the TUI table picker pre-filled with those suggestions. Watch the new connector land in the TUI (:runs) — see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Sync a table incrementally on a watermark
docs.text:
spec:
  source:
    tables:
      - name: invoices
        mode: watermark
        watermark_column: updated_at
        pk_columns: [invoice_id]

Result: each run reads only the rows whose updated_at (or, on a tie, primary key) is past the persisted cursor — a full first run, then only what changed since. Watch it land in the TUI (:runs) — see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Full-dump a reference table nightly
docs.text:
spec:
  source:
    tables:
      - name: customers
        mode: full
        pk_columns: [customer_id]
  schedule: "0 6 * * *"   # daily at 06:00
  window: "22:00-07:00"   # optional — scheduled runs only fire inside it (UTC; end exclusive, so 07:00 keeps the 06:00 slot in)

Result: every run re-scans the table chunk by chunk in primary-key order, resumable if interrupted — inserts are always picked up, but a row changed in place is only ever re-read on mode: watermark. Watch it land in the TUI (:runs) — see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Index the hub table for fast métier queries
docs.text:
spec:
  source:
    tables:
      - name: invoices
        mode: watermark
        watermark_column: updated_at
        pk_columns: [invoice_id]
        indexes:
          - { columns: [customer_id], unique: false }

Result: the declared Postgres index is created on connector.t_invoices at apply time. Watch it land in the TUI (:runs) — see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Rename a source column that collides with a hub system column
docs.text:
spec:
  source:
    tables:
      - name: invoices
        mode: watermark
        watermark_column: updated_at
        pk_columns: [invoice_id]
        rename:
          id: source_id

Result: the source's id column lands in the hub table as source_id — same values, different column name; nothing changes on the source database. Watch it land in the TUI (:runs) — see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Gesture run fails: password_env ... unset the variable must exist in the hub server's environment, not the laptop's — jdbc does not consult lm secret export the variable where the hub itself runs watermark never advances / rows keep re-reading watermark_column isn't actually updated by the source app on every change pick a truly-monotonic column, using discover's suggested watermark updated rows never re-ingested in mode: full by design — the PK-only cursor captures inserts, never re-reads on update switch that table to mode: watermark run fails: source column 'id' collides with a hub system column a source column shares one of the seven reserved hub-column names (id is the common one) add rename: { id: source_id } under that table (or defaults:) — see How to above

docs.title: Kafka
docs.text:
lumnik Pro. Consume a Kafka-compatible topic (Kafka, Redpanda, Azure Event Hubs) into a hub table: each run catches up to the head and completes; the hub owns the offsets.

Type kafka Protocol Kafka wire (JSON messages) Target connector.t_<name> Schedulable cron Edition Pro

Not available in the open edition — the connector type is absent there and a kafka manifest is refused at validate.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
# 10-kafka-json.yaml — plaintext Kafka source: one topic, JSON messages, no auth.
#
# Apply and run:
#   lm apply -f docs/connectors/kafka/10-kafka-json.yaml
#   lm connector run kafka-erp-exports
#
# How this connector works
# -------------------------
# No Kafka consumer group is created or needed — the hub tracks each
# partition's read position itself, the same way it tracks a JDBC watermark.
# A run catches up chunk by chunk until it reaches the head of the topic,
# then completes.
#
# Non-JSON messages are set aside (not lost) and never block the run — the
# same per-row safety net as the CSV connector's dead-letter queue.
#
# Dedup: re-ingesting the same message is silently skipped, so producers can
# retry safely without creating duplicate rows.
#
# Auth: none — no SASL credentials are sent; suitable for a local Redpanda or
# an internal broker that trusts the network.

apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: kafka-erp-exports            # unique connector name within the workspace
  connector_type: kafka              # selects the Kafka connector implementation
  scopes: [demo]

spec:
  name: erp_events                   # logical/table name → target table connector.t_erp_events

  brokers: localhost:9092            # Kafka / Redpanda bootstrap address (literal)
  # brokers_env: KAFKA_BROKERS       # alternative: resolve from env var

  topic: erp-exports                 # source topic; must be identifier-safe (no spaces)

  format: json                       # v1: one JSON object per message (Avro/Protobuf deferred)

  # No auth block → unauthenticated connection (no SASL handshake).

lm validate -f docs/connectors/kafka/10-kafka-json.yaml
lm apply -f docs/connectors/kafka/10-kafka-json.yaml
lm connector run kafka-erp-exports

docs.title: How it behaves
docs.text:
• A run catches up, chunk by chunk. The engine loops chunks within one run — each chunk is one consumer poll batch, written in its own transaction — until an empty poll says the topic is caught up, which completes the run. Each message's top-level JSON fields become table columns in connector.t_<name> (schema inferred automatically, the same auto-schema behavior as JDBC and CSV). Kafka manifests carry no mapping hooks — there is no spec.mapping block on this connector type; see Transformers for what a mapping block would do on a connector that supports it.
  • First run = full-retention ingest: a partition (one ordered slice of the topic) with no stored cursor seeks to the beginning, so run #1 reads everything the topic still retains. Subsequent runs resume at the stored partition→offset (each partition's saved read position) cursor.
  • Non-JSON messages go to the per-message DLQ (MalformedSource) and never block ingestion — the same discipline as the CSV per-row DLQ. Their offsets still advance: a poison message is dead-lettered once and never re-read. A poll of only poison keeps polling for real rows, bounded by the chunk budget, so even a continuously-poison topic cannot wedge a run — the advanced cursor is persisted and the next run resumes past the poison.
  • Dedup by content hash (_row_hash): re-ingesting the same message is a silent conflict; data.row.changed fires only for genuinely-new rows.
  • Seven column names are reserved. id, _row_hash, _ingested_at, _source, _run_id, _mapping_version, tenant_id — the hub adds these to every connector.t_<name> table. A top-level JSON field sharing one of them is refused at write time, on a brand-new table and on one that already exists alike. Because kafka manifests carry no mapping hooks, there is no in-product rename here: the field has to reach the hub under another name, which means changing what the producer puts on the topic. id is the one you will meet.

docs.title: Field reference
docs.text:
Field Required Meaning name yes logical/table name → connector.t_<name> brokers or brokers_env one of the two bootstrap servers, literal or via env var topic yes must match [a-zA-Z0-9._-]+ format no v1 supports only json (Avro/Protobuf deferred) — one JSON object per message poll_timeout_ms no consumer poll timeout, range [100, 60000], default 2000 max_poll_records no max records per consumer poll; positive integer, default 500; clamped to the engine chunk size (500) auth no kind: none (default) or kind: sasl-plain with username_env + password_env (+ optional security_protocol) metadata.scopes no the métier scope(s) the topic's rows are askable in — see Scopes for chat

With sasl-plain, auth.security_protocol overrides the wire protocol — default SASL_SSL; set SASL_PLAINTEXT for a SASL broker without TLS. The value lands verbatim in the consumer's security.protocol (it is not validated at apply time).

One connector reads one topic, and this release has no message-key or header filtering — whatever the topic carries lands whole in that connector's table. If a topic multiplexes several event types together, give each event stream its own topic when you need them separated into different tables.

docs.title: Scopes for chat
docs.text: Declare scopes: [...] under metadata to make ingested rows discoverable in scoped chat — the same field, and the same validate-time warning when it is missing, as every other connector kind.

docs.title: Continuous consumption
docs.text: A run is a catch-up, not a subscription: it drains the backlog to the head and completes. To keep the table current, declare a schedule: cron in the manifest — like jdbc/csv/rest, it lands on the scheduler (absent cron on re-apply = unschedule). Each run resumes at the stored cursor and catches up again. Overlap is safe: a submission while a run is already active on the endpoint is skipped (per-endpoint advisory lock), so an aggressive cadence degrades to back-to-back catch-ups, never double ingestion. An external trigger works too: cron + lm connector run <name>.

docs.title: Azure Event Hubs — the event-hubs preset
docs.text:
Vendor presets ride as spec.preset while connector_type stays kafka. The preset pre-wires the bootstrap address (<namespace>.servicebus.windows.net:9093) and SASL/SSL from the connection string. No Kafka consumer group is created or needed here either — the hub tracks offsets itself, same as any other kafka connector, so there's nothing to provision or clean up on the Event Hubs side.

Prerequisite — two env vars where the hub runs. Event Hubs' Kafka endpoint authenticates as SASL/PLAIN with the fixed username $ConnectionString (the literal string, dollar sign included — it is not a secret) and the namespace connection string as the password. The preset reads the username from the fixed env var EVENT_HUBS_SASL_USERNAME and the password from the env var you name in connection_string_env; both resolve from the process environment only (OS env, then JVM system property) — the lm secret store is not consulted:

export EVENTHUBS_CONN_STR='Endpoint=sb://…'           # the namespace Primary Connection String
export EVENT_HUBS_SASL_USERNAME='$ConnectionString'   # the fixed literal username

# 20-event-hubs.yaml — Azure Event Hubs via the 'event-hubs' vendor preset.
#
# Apply and run:
#   lm apply -f docs/connectors/kafka/20-event-hubs.yaml
#   lm connector run event-hubs-telemetry
#
# How the event-hubs preset works
# --------------------------------
# connector_type stays 'kafka' — the preset just pre-wires the bootstrap
# address (namespace.servicebus.windows.net:9093) and SASL/SSL settings from
# the connection string, so you don't have to work those out by hand. No
# Kafka consumer group is created or needed — the hub tracks offsets itself,
# same as any other kafka connector.
#
# The 'connection_string_env' field names an env var that holds the Event Hubs
# connection string (Primary Connection String from the Azure portal). Kafka resolves
# *_env via the process environment only (OS env, then JVM system property) — the
# lm secret store is NOT consulted here. Export it where the hub runs:
#   export EVENTHUBS_CONN_STR="Endpoint=sb://..."
#
# Auth: Event Hubs over Kafka uses SASL/PLAIN with fixed username "$ConnectionString".
# Set it once in the environment (it is not a secret):
#   export EVENT_HUBS_SASL_USERNAME='$ConnectionString'

apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: event-hubs-telemetry         # unique connector name within the workspace
  connector_type: kafka              # real engine type; the vendor alias is spec.preset below
  scopes: [demo, azure]

spec:
  preset: event-hubs                 # vendor preset — expands to a real kafka config at apply time

  name: telemetry_events             # logical/table name → target table connector.t_telemetry_events

  namespace: my-namespace            # Azure Event Hubs namespace (without .servicebus.windows.net)

  connection_string_env: EVENTHUBS_CONN_STR   # env var holding the Primary Connection String

  topic: telemetry                   # Event Hub name (= Kafka topic name)

  format: json                       # v1: one JSON object per message

An unknown preset name is rejected at validate time (a typo never silently degrades to plain kafka), and a preset missing its inputs (e.g. namespace) reports each missing field before expansion.

docs.title: Keep a topic mirrored on a cadence
docs.text:
spec:
  schedule: "*/5 * * * *"   # every 5 minutes

Result: each scheduled run resumes at the stored partition→offset cursor and catches up to the head again. A submission while a run is already active on the endpoint is skipped (per-endpoint advisory lock) — an aggressive cadence degrades to back-to-back catch-ups, never double ingestion. Watch it land in the TUI (CLI & TUI): :runs for the run's status.

docs.title: Connect Azure Event Hubs
docs.text:
export EVENTHUBS_CONN_STR='Endpoint=sb://…'           # the namespace Primary Connection String
export EVENT_HUBS_SASL_USERNAME='$ConnectionString'   # the fixed literal username

# 20-event-hubs.yaml — Azure Event Hubs via the 'event-hubs' vendor preset.
#
# Apply and run:
#   lm apply -f docs/connectors/kafka/20-event-hubs.yaml
#   lm connector run event-hubs-telemetry

# How the event-hubs preset works
# --------------------------------
# connector_type stays 'kafka' — the preset just pre-wires the bootstrap
# address (namespace.servicebus.windows.net:9093) and SASL/SSL settings from
# the connection string, so you don't have to work those out by hand. No
# Kafka consumer group is created or needed — the hub tracks offsets itself,
# same as any other kafka connector.
#
# The 'connection_string_env' field names an env var that holds the Event Hubs
# connection string (Primary Connection String from the Azure portal). Kafka resolves
# *_env via the process environment only (OS env, then JVM system property) — the
# lm secret store is NOT consulted here. Export it where the hub runs:
#   export EVENTHUBS_CONN_STR="Endpoint=sb://..."
#
# Auth: Event Hubs over Kafka uses SASL/PLAIN with fixed username "$ConnectionString".
# Set it once in the environment (it is not a secret):
#   export EVENT_HUBS_SASL_USERNAME='$ConnectionString'

apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: event-hubs-telemetry         # unique connector name within the workspace
  connector_type: kafka              # real engine type; the vendor alias is spec.preset below
  scopes: [demo, azure]

spec:
  preset: event-hubs                 # vendor preset — expands to a real kafka config at apply time

  name: telemetry_events             # logical/table name → target table connector.t_telemetry_events

  namespace: my-namespace            # Azure Event Hubs namespace (without .servicebus.windows.net)

  connection_string_env: EVENTHUBS_CONN_STR   # env var holding the Primary Connection String

  topic: telemetry                   # Event Hub name (= Kafka topic name)

  format: json                       # v1: one JSON object per message

Result: lm connector run event-hubs-telemetry connects over SASL/PLAIN using the two exported variables and catches the Event Hub up into connector.t_telemetry_events. Watch it land in the TUI (CLI & TUI): :runs.

docs.title: Inspect messages that failed to ingest
docs.text:
lm dlq list
lm dlq get <id>

Result: every non-JSON message is dead-lettered under reason MalformedSource, one entry per message, and its offset still advances so the run never stalls behind it. Watch the queue in the TUI (CLI & TUI): :dlq.

docs.text: Symptom Cause Gesture first run ingests far more than expected no stored cursor yet = a full-retention read, by design let it complete — later runs are incremental non-JSON messages missing from the target table dead-lettered per message; offsets still advance lm dlq list auth failure against Event Hubs username must be the literal $ConnectionString via EVENT_HUBS_SASL_USERNAME; password comes from connection_string_env — both resolve from the process environment only export both where the hub runs a run never seems to "subscribe" a run is a catch-up, not a subscription schedule a cron run fails: source column 'id' collides with a hub system column a top-level field shares one of the seven reserved names; kafka has no mapping hooks, so nothing can rename it inside lumnik the producer must emit that field under another name — see How it behaves

docs.title: REST
docs.text:
Ingest any HTTP/JSON API into hybrid JSONB + typed columns: point at the base URL, declare endpoints and pagination, apply.

Type rest-generic Protocol HTTP/JSON (+ GraphQL & SOAP shapes) Target ext.<connector>_<endpoint> Schedulable cron Edition Open

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
Installer demo path? See docs/quickstart/installer.md for the 60-second sequence (Stripe / CSV / combined).

# 1. Generate manifest from an OpenAPI spec
lm source rest from-openapi \
    https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stripe/openapi/master/openapi/spec3.json \
    --name stripe --scope billing --output stripe.yaml

# 2. Review and adjust (auth, pagination, schedule — the cron lands on the hub scheduler)
$EDITOR stripe.yaml

# 3. Apply
lm apply -f stripe.yaml

# 4. Run the connector
lm connector run stripe

docs.title: YAML manifest
docs.text:
apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: stripe
  connector_type: rest-generic
  scopes: [billing]
spec:
  base_url: https://api.stripe.com
  auth:
    kind: bearer
    token_env: STRIPE_API_KEY
  default_rate_limit: 100/s
  schedule: "0 6 * * *"     # optional cron expression, daily at 06:00 UTC — the hub scheduler fires it
  endpoints:
    - id: charges
      method: GET
      path: /v1/charges
      pagination:
        kind: cursor
        cursor_param: starting_after
        cursor_path: $.data[-1:].id
        has_more_path: $.has_more
        response_path: $.data
      incremental: { mode: full }
      target:
        kind: hybrid
        table: ext.stripe_charges
        unique_key: $.id
        promote:
          - { name: amount,   path: $.amount,   type: bigint }
          - { name: currency, path: $.currency, type: text }
          - { name: status,   path: $.status,   type: text }

Each endpoint declares id (kebab-case), method (one of GET | POST | PUT | PATCH | DELETE), path, a pagination block and a target block; incremental is optional (defaults to full). schedule (spec-level, shown above) is optional too — omit it to run only on demand with lm connector run.

The path-shaped fields (cursor_path, has_more_path, response_path, unique_key, …) are JSONPath expressions read against the response body: $ is the root, so $.data[-1:].id reads "the id of the last element of data".

Each target.promote entry may also carry an optional transform:, applied as the value is written — see Transformers for the full list.

docs.title: Pagination strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Use for Required fields Optional fields (default) cursor Stripe, OpenAI, most modern APIs cursor_param, cursor_path, has_more_path, response_path cursor_binding (query) page Spring HATEOAS, Laravel page_param, response_path size_param, size (50), start_page (1), total_pages_path, has_more_path, last_path, empty_check (true) offset Legacy REST offset_param, limit_param, response_path limit (100), total_path link-header GitHub, JSON:API response_path rel (next) relay GraphQL Connections cursor_path, has_more_path, response_path; plus cursor_param (query/header binding) or cursor_var (variable binding) cursor_binding (query) body-link Django REST, JSON:API, NestJS, HATEOAS link_path, response_path — custom Anything weird response_path Kotlin script (deferred to a future release)

page stops on whichever of total_pages_path / has_more_path / last_path is present — and, with empty_check: true (the default), on the first empty page.

docs.title: Cursor binding
docs.text:
For cursor and relay, cursor_binding picks where the next-page cursor is injected:

Binding Cursor goes into Needs query (default) a query parameter cursor_param header an HTTP header cursor_param (the header name) variable the POST body's variables.<name> cursor_var — relay on a graphql endpoint only

variable is refused outside relay on a graphql endpoint (the cursor rides a POST body that a plain GET never sends); conversely, graphql endpoints require exactly relay + variable.

Pure GraphQL APIs (POST a query, cursor in variables): see GraphQL.

docs.title: Pagination presets
docs.text:
Modern APIs follow well-known conventions — declare one preset instead of the full block. A preset expands to a real strategy on lm apply.

Preset For Expands to spring-page Spring Data Page page ($.content, $.totalPages, 0-indexed) spring-slice Spring Data Slice (no total) page + last_path: $.last spring-hateoas Spring Data REST body-link ($._links.next.href, $._embedded.{items} — needs items) micronaut Micronaut Data Page page ($.content, $.totalPages) drf-page Django REST PageNumberPagination body-link ($.next, $.results) drf-limit-offset Django REST LimitOffsetPagination offset ($.count, $.results) fastapi fastapi-pagination page ($.items, $.pages, 1-indexed) nestjs nestjs-paginate body-link ($.links.next, $.data) json-api JSON:API body-link ($.links.next, $.data) sequelize Node/Sequelize offset ($.count, $.rows) stripe Stripe-style cursor cursor ($.has_more, $.data) 
pagination: { kind: spring-page }                       # 7 lines → 1
pagination: { kind: spring-page, size: 50 }             # override any field
pagination: { kind: spring-hateoas, items: products }   # {items} → $._embedded.products

body-link is also a first-class strategy: { kind: body-link, link_path: $.next, response_path: $.results } follows a next URL from the response body until it is null.

docs.title: Auth providers
docs.text:
Kind Config bearer token_env: VAR_NAME (preferred), or token_value: "..." (dev only) basic username + password_env: VAR_NAME api-key in: header\|query, name, value_env: VAR_NAME none no credentials (the default when auth: is omitted)

Every auth *_env field (the fields of the providers in this section) resolves an lm secret name first, then falls back to a server environment variable / JVM system property of that name. Set the value before lm apply:

lm secret set STRIPE_API_KEY -   # paste the value on stdin, Ctrl+D

OAuth2 (client_credentials, authorization_code), HMAC, and mTLS are dedicated future projects.

docs.title: Request headers
docs.text:
Connector-level only — spec.headers[] is applied to every request:

spec:
  headers:
    - { name: X-Api-Version, value: "2024-10" }       # static
    - { name: X-Client-Id,   value_env: CLIENT_ID }   # from the environment
  • Each entry needs name + exactly one of value / value_env.
  • value_env resolves the OS environment first, then a JVM system property.
  • Headers are applied before auth — auth-injected headers win on a name clash.
  • Endpoint-level headers are refused at apply ("per-endpoint headers are not supported in this release; declare headers at spec.headers").

docs.title: Reliability
docs.text:
• Retry — fixed policy, not a manifest knob: up to 5 attempts per request on HTTP 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 408 and on network errors; exponential backoff 1s → 2s → 4s → … capped at 60s, ±10% jitter; a numeric Retry-After header overrides the computed delay. Any other status is returned as-is, no retry.
  • Page cap — the pagination loop stops after 10 000 pages per endpoint per run (MAX_PAGES), a runaway-loop guard.
  • Rate limit — default_rate_limit (default 100/s) is a count/window string; the window is an optional integer + unit s|m|h (100/s, 100/5m, 1000/h). Declared once at connector level: one token bucket per connector, shared by all its endpoints — no per-endpoint override. In practice: with several endpoints on one connector, set it to the strictest endpoint's documented limit — a laxer value lets the busier endpoints starve it.

docs.title: Incremental sync
docs.text:
incremental:
  mode: full              # always re-fetch all pages (default)
  # OR
  mode: watermark         # send the stored watermark as a query param,
  param: updated_since    #   e.g. ?updated_since=<watermark>
  watermark_path: $.updated   # new watermark = MAX of this JsonPath over the items

mode: api_cursor (API-native cursor persistence) is deferred — not implemented; declaring it today behaves like full.

Cursor state is stored in connector.connector_cursor per endpoint and survives runs.

docs.title: Storage layout
docs.text:
Nothing to set up here — each endpoint's table is created automatically. Rows land as the typed promoted columns plus the full JSONB payload, and re-syncs are safe to re-run (they upsert, never duplicate). The rest of this section is reference, for when you need it.

Each endpoint writes to a dynamically created ext.<connector>_<endpoint> table:

CREATE TABLE ext.stripe_charges (
    id            BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,
    external_id   TEXT NOT NULL,
    -- promoted typed columns:
    amount        BIGINT,
    currency      TEXT,
    status        TEXT,
    -- always:
    data          JSONB NOT NULL,
    indexed_at    TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(),
    connector_id  UUID NOT NULL,
    endpoint_id   UUID NOT NULL,
    UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON ext.stripe_charges USING GIN (data jsonb_path_ops);

UNIQUE (tenant_id, external_id) + ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is the mechanism behind that upsert.

Deleting a REST connector deletes its data

lm connector delete drops the connector's registered ext.* hybrid tables along with any connector.t_* dynamic tables, and every RAG chunk the connector produced dies with it — the same erasure gesture as the other connector families. To empty one endpoint's rows without deleting the connector, use lm endpoint purge <connector>/<endpoint>.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
lm apply -f <file.yaml>
lm endpoint enable|disable|reset-cursor|purge <connector>/<endpoint>
lm connector run <connector>
lm source rest test <connector>                     # pre-flight: auth + 1 page, no write
lm source rest from-openapi <url> --name N --scope S -o FILE
lm source rest probe <connector> --endpoint <path>   # sample fetch + manifest draft

docs.text:

Full reference: CLI & TUI.

docs.text:
lm source rest from-openapi \

Result: a manifest scaffold (stripe.yaml) with endpoints inferred from the OpenAPI spec — review auth, pagination, and target before lm apply.

docs.title: Start from a pagination preset
docs.text:
pagination: { kind: spring-page }                       # 7 lines → 1
pagination: { kind: spring-page, size: 50 }             # override any field
pagination: { kind: spring-hateoas, items: products }   # {items} → $._embedded.products

Result: the preset expands into a full pagination block at lm apply — see Pagination presets for the full list.

docs.title: Reset a stuck cursor
docs.text:
lm endpoint reset-cursor <connector>/<endpoint>

Result: the next lm connector run <connector> is a full refresh — watch it land in the TUI (:runs), or see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Add a typed column later
docs.text:
Add an entry to the endpoint's target.promote list, then re-apply:

promote:
  - { name: amount,   path: $.amount,   type: bigint }
  - { name: currency, path: $.currency, type: text }   # new column

lm apply -f stripe.yaml

Result: the next lm connector run does ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN — no existing data is rewritten. Check the run in the TUI (:runs), or see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Gesture 429 Too Many Requests from the API default_rate_limit exceeds what the API tolerates lower it (e.g. 100/s → 50/s) Cursor stuck — sync stops picking up new pages the stored cursor is stale or invalid lm endpoint reset-cursor <connector>/<endpoint> → next run is a full refresh lm apply refused with an unknown transform a promote entry's transform: isn't one of the supported values see Transformers for the supported list Need to wipe an endpoint's data — lm endpoint purge <connector>/<endpoint> (requires confirmation) Not sure the token/auth is valid — lm source rest test <connector> — pre-flight check, fetches 1 page, writes nothing

docs.title: SOAP
docs.text:
Ingest legacy SOAP services (Siebel, SAP PI) with a templated <soap:Body> and QueryPage-style pagination — a request shape on the REST engine.

Type rest-generic (shape soap) Protocol SOAP 1.1 over POST Target ext.* hybrid Schedulable cron Edition Open

Auth, rate-limiting, retry, and storage are all shared with REST — this page covers only what's different: the body template, QueryPage pagination, and fault handling.

docs.title: Full example — Siebel QueryPage
docs.text:
The real, validator-true manifest (the same file the tests exercise):

# Siebel CustomerQueryPage over SOAP, exposed as a canonical hub table.
# kind: soap is a request-shape on the HTTP engine (connector_type stays rest-generic).
apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: siebel-customers
  connector_type: rest-generic
  scopes: [crm, customers, siebel]
spec:
  base_url: https://siebel.example.com
  auth:
    kind: basic
    username: siebel_svc          # literal username (the basic block reads `username`, not an env)
    password_env: SIEBEL_PWD      # env var name holding the password
  endpoints:
    - id: customers
      kind: soap
      path: /eai_enu/start.swe
      soap_action: "document/urn:crmod:...:CustomerQueryPage"
      body: |
        <CustomerQueryPage_Input>
          <PageSize>{{page_size}}</PageSize>
          <StartRowNum>{{cursor}}</StartRowNum>
          <ListOfCustomer><Customer><Id query="*"/><Name query="*"/></Customer></ListOfCustomer>
        </CustomerQueryPage_Input>
      pagination:
        kind: soap
        page_size: 100
        last_page_path: "$.Body.CustomerQueryPage_Output.LastPage"
        response_path: "$.Body.CustomerQueryPage_Output.ListOfCustomer.Customer"
      target:
        kind: hybrid
        table: ext.siebel_customers
        unique_key: "$.Id"
        promote:
          - { name: name, path: "$.Name", type: text }

docs.title: Endpoint fields (kind: soap)
docs.text:
Field Required Meaning id yes endpoint identifier (kebab-case) path yes POST target, relative to base_url body yes the inner <soap:Body> XML template (lumnik wraps the SOAP 1.1 envelope) soap_action no sent as the SOAPAction header header no inner <soap:Header> XML template pagination.kind: soap yes see below — kind: soap endpoints require it, and vice-versa

Method is implicitly POST with Content-Type: text/xml. The engine sends SOAP 1.1 envelopes only — a service that requires SOAP 1.2 (application/soap+xml) is not supported in this release.

docs.title: Body templating
docs.text:
Placeholders resolved on every request — in body: and header: alike, same substitution:

  • {{page_size}} / {{cursor}} — pagination state. cursor is the row offset, starting at 0: the QueryPage example's {{cursor}} therefore sends 0 (StartRowNum) on the first request, then advances by page_size each page.
  • {{secret:NAME}} / {{env:NAME}} — both resolve from the hub's process environment (OS env var first, JVM system property as dev/test fallback). The DB-backed lm secret registry is not consulted here — export the variable where the hub runs.

An unresolved placeholder fails the run fast — a template is never sent with a literal {{...}} left inside. header: is optional — use it when the service expects auth or session elements inside <soap:Header> rather than in the body.

docs.title: Connector-level headers
docs.text: spec.headers[] applies to SOAP endpoints too — the entries ride every page of the QueryPage loop. Applied before auth (auth-injected headers win on a name clash); Content-Type and SOAPAction are set by the engine, so don't redeclare them. Endpoint-level headers are refused at apply, exactly as for REST endpoints.

docs.title: Pagination (kind: soap)
docs.text:
Offset arithmetic in the QueryPage style:

Field Required Meaning page_size yes rows per page; injected as {{page_size}} — explicit, no default response_path yes plain dotted path to the repeated element (e.g. $.Body.Out.ListOf.Customer) last_page_path no path to a boolean "this is the last page" has_more_path no path to a boolean "there are more pages"

One stop signal applies — chosen by configuration, not tried in sequence:

  • last_page_path set → it is authoritative: pagination continues only while the flag is explicitly false; a true, missing, or null flag stops (never loops forever).
  • else has_more_path set → continues only while explicitly true; missing/null stops.
  • else → stop on a page shorter than page_size.

(Flags arrive as XML strings — "true"/"false" are accepted as booleans.)

page_size is deliberately defaultless: a silent default that mismatched the service's real page size would skip or duplicate rows wherever the body template uses {{page_size}}. The validator requires the key; a non-positive or non-numeric value fails the run fast, before any request is sent.

response_path must be a plain dotted path

JsonPath operators ([*], ..) are rejected by the validator for SOAP pagination — with the XML-to-tree conversion they would silently match a single element and lose data.

docs.title: Response handling
docs.text:
• XXE-hardened: DTDs and external entities are disabled in the XML parser.
  • Namespace prefixes are stripped (ns1:Customer → Customer) before path matching.
  • The terminal segment of response_path is force-listed — one <Customer> or fifty, you always get a list. (v1 limit: intermediate repeated segments are not coerced.)
  • A SOAP Fault fails the run (no partial ingestion) — and is never retried: SOAP 1.1 faults arrive with HTTP 500, but the fault check runs before status-based retry, so a fault is treated as a business error, not a transient one.
  • Plain HTTP failures retry as transient on exactly 429, 500, 502, 503, 504, 408 (plus network errors) — the shared REST policy. Every other status (501, 505, any other 4xx, …) is permanent.

docs.title: Connect a Siebel QueryPage service
docs.text:
Point path at the SOAP endpoint, template the inner <soap:Body> with {{page_size}} / {{cursor}}, and set pagination.kind: soap with a response_path that names the repeated element:

# Siebel CustomerQueryPage over SOAP, exposed as a canonical hub table.
# kind: soap is a request-shape on the HTTP engine (connector_type stays rest-generic).
apiVersion: connectors.lumnik.io/v1
kind: Connector
metadata:
  name: siebel-customers
  connector_type: rest-generic
  scopes: [crm, customers, siebel]
spec:
  base_url: https://siebel.example.com
  auth:
    kind: basic
    username: siebel_svc          # literal username (the basic block reads `username`, not an env)
    password_env: SIEBEL_PWD      # env var name holding the password
  endpoints:
    - id: customers
      kind: soap
      path: /eai_enu/start.swe
      soap_action: "document/urn:crmod:...:CustomerQueryPage"
      body: |
        <CustomerQueryPage_Input>
          <PageSize>{{page_size}}</PageSize>
          <StartRowNum>{{cursor}}</StartRowNum>
          <ListOfCustomer><Customer><Id query="*"/><Name query="*"/></Customer></ListOfCustomer>
        </CustomerQueryPage_Input>
      pagination:
        kind: soap
        page_size: 100
        last_page_path: "$.Body.CustomerQueryPage_Output.LastPage"
        response_path: "$.Body.CustomerQueryPage_Output.ListOfCustomer.Customer"
      target:
        kind: hybrid
        table: ext.siebel_customers
        unique_key: "$.Id"
        promote:
          - { name: name, path: "$.Name", type: text }

Result: lm apply -f siebel-customers.yaml registers the connector; lm connector run siebel-customers walks the QueryPage loop offset by offset, writing rows into ext.siebel_customers. Watch it land in the TUI (:runs), or see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Pass a secret into the body template
docs.text:
Any field in body: (or header:) can carry {{secret:NAME}} or {{env:NAME}} alongside the pagination placeholders — for example, an API token woven into the Siebel body above:

body: |
  <CustomerQueryPage_Input>
    <PageSize>{{page_size}}</PageSize>
    <StartRowNum>{{cursor}}</StartRowNum>
    <ApiToken>{{env:NAME}}</ApiToken>
    <ListOfCustomer><Customer><Id query="*"/><Name query="*"/></Customer></ListOfCustomer>
  </CustomerQueryPage_Input>

{{env:NAME}} (and {{secret:NAME}}) resolve from the hub's process environment — an OS env var, or a JVM system property as a dev/test fallback. This is not the lm secret registry: export the variable where the hub process itself runs, e.g.:

export NAME=...

Result: the placeholder is substituted into the request body on every call; if the variable isn't set where the hub runs, the run fails fast rather than sending a literal {{env:NAME}}. Check the run in the TUI (:runs), or see CLI & TUI.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Gesture Run fails immediately with an unresolved {{...}} the placeholder name isn't found in the hub's process environment export it where the hub runs (OS env var, or a JVM system property for dev/test) Run fails on HTTP 500 with no retry a SOAP Fault is a business error, not a transient one — it is never retried fix the request; faults are not retried by design Pagination loops or stops early the wrong stop signal is set (or two conflicting ones) set exactly one of last_page_path / has_more_path — or rely on the short-page fallback by setting neither response_path rejected at validate JsonPath operators ([*], ..) are refused for SOAP pagination use a plain dotted path only (e.g. $.Body.Out.ListOf.Customer)
