Password guessing — is brute force throttled at the login? This page Yes, on by default: both shipped realms set bruteForceProtected: true — Keycloak temporarily locks an account after repeated failures (Keycloak defaults: lockout after ~30 failures, waits growing to 15 minutes, never permanent). Tune or inspect it in the console: realm lumnik → Realm settings → Security defenses → Brute force detection. With your own IdP, this layer is your IdP's policy, not lumnik's. Deprovisioning — does a departure in our IdP actually cut access? SCIM deprovisioning → Why SCIM push closes the loop: the request right after active:false is denied, even with a still-valid token. SCIM is not in the open edition — see the note below. Secrets at rest — are stored credentials encrypted? RLS & database roles → Secrets at rest Yes — pgcrypto, AES-256, one master key. No rotation tooling: losing the key makes the secrets it protects unrecoverable. Data at rest — is our ingested data encrypted in the database? RLS & database roles → Data at rest No. Only secrets and connector credentials are ciphered; your mirrored rows and the RAG corpus are plaintext PostgreSQL columns. Volume/disk and backup encryption are your layer. Data in transit — is traffic encrypted end-to-end? RLS & database roles → Data in transit The hub itself speaks plain HTTP; TLS terminates at whichever edge you put in front (the optional Caddy façade, your own reverse proxy, or the k8s Gateway). Behind that edge — hub↔PostgreSQL, hub↔Ollama, façade↔hub — everything rides your internal network in the clear. Securing that network is the operator's layer. Personal data & erasure — can we honour access and erasure requests? GDPR & personal data → The rights, in practice Access and rectification are real, if manual. No one-click DSAR export; erasure of ingested data is a documented rebuild procedure, not an automated one. Audit trail — who did what, when? GDPR & personal data → Where personal data can live Narrow, but real — with two gaps. Recorded with the acting user: User writes (non-SCIM), Secret writes, view/workflow applies (with the manifest's SHA-256), and entity reads. Not recorded: SCIM-driven User writes — deprovisioning included. The full answer. Inbound rate limits — can one tenant or a runaway client exhaust our capacity? Inbound rate limits → What is limited The LLM-backed endpoints are capped per tenant, per 60s window; CRUD, views and ingestion are unlimited. Single-node only — the counters live in the hub process. Backup & restore — can we recover from data loss? Backup & restore (self-host) Yes, scripted, hot for PostgreSQL. No point-in-time recovery — nightly snapshots only. Vulnerability disclosure — how do we report an issue, and is there a patch SLA? SECURITY.md, at the root of every edition Email contact@lumnik.fr, subject [lumnik security], never a public issue — 72-hour acknowledgment, 14-day fix-or-mitigation answer. The same file ships in every edition. Dependency updates have their own watch posture: the full answer. Source-mirror retention — how long are ingested rows kept? This page No retention policy — kept indefinitely. Unlike the event outbox (lumnik.events.retention-days, 30 days by default, purged nightly — GDPR & personal data), nothing schedules a purge of connector.t_* mirror tables or rag.chunk: rows persist until the connector is deleted (DynamicTableRegistry.purgeForConnector) or removed by hand. PII in application logs — does the hub log personal data? Not comprehensively documented Partially answered: the login path deliberately keeps IdP subject/issuer out of WARN-level logs (TenantContextFilter.java:208, ExternalIdentityCreator.java:49,64), and chat/search log only counts and tenant/source, never message or row content (RetrievalService.java:175). There is no repo-wide log-content policy or audit — Reading the logs itself warns that DEBUG "may echo data you would rather not keep." Open question.

docs.title: Which edition — the full answer
docs.text:
GET /api/platform/health lists the manifest-bearing modules on the classpath — the four that declare a META-INF/module-manifest.yaml: core, identity, rag and llm. An open-edition install answers core and identity only; a build carrying the chat extensions also answers rag (the doors) and llm (the model provider).

Both halves have to be there, and the two layers say it differently:

  • the métier PWA reads this same list and treats either half missing as chat not installed — no input is shown at all;
  • called directly, a rag-without-llm build answers the door and then fails at the model call (AskToSqlAgent resolves its ChatPort only at the generation step), rather than answering 404 as an open-edition build does.

The hub logs the same list at boot (Platform loaded N module(s): …). What this row decides: identity federation, deprovisioning, the audit trail's SCIM gap, the rate-limit buckets, everything naming rag.chunk, the disclosure row, and the whole Edition boundary block in the gaps.

docs.title: Audit trail — the full answer
docs.text:
Recorded in core.audit_event, each row with the acting user:

  • User writes (non-SCIM): login, email, locked, default scope.
  • Secret writes: create, rotate, delete — never the ciphertext or plaintext value.
  • View / workflow applies: actor, name, scope, and the manifest's SHA-256 — an auditor can prove which YAML was applied even though the store keeps only the latest.
  • Entity reads via GET /api/entities/{name}.

The two named gaps: archiving a user IS recorded but only as an indistinguishable UPDATE; SCIM-driven User writes — deprovisioning included — are not recorded at all (a tenant-context mismatch between the SCIM auth filter and the audit listener). Every other entity still no-ops, and there is no read surface — an auditor queries core.audit_event directly. See the gap below.

docs.title: Dependency watch — the full answer
docs.text:
Since 2026-08-22, .github/dependabot.yml opens one grouped pull request a week (Monday) for GitHub Actions, the Go modules under lm/ (otk-unit.yml runs the Go suite on the pull request) and the docs' pip pin (docs-publish.yml rebuilds with --strict and runs the render check).

How much the pull request verifies is uneven for the Actions half, and the file says so: only three workflows run on pull_request, so only actions/checkout, actions/setup-go and actions/setup-python are exercised by the PR proposing their bump. setup-java and upload-artifact can be reached by dispatching otk-battery.yml on the branch; the four docker/* actions (hub-image.yml, push only) and goreleaser (lm-release.yml, tags only) cannot be reached before a merge at all. They stay watched anyway — a SHA pin that nothing bumps rots in silence — but watched is not verified.

Maven — 160 direct dependencies — and the Dockerfile base images are deliberately left unwatched, each named with its reason inside that file: no pull-request job compiles or tests Java (nightly-verify.yml runs on cron, after a merge), and hub-image.yml builds on push to main rather than on pull_request. A bot opening pull requests that nothing can check would only teach us to merge a green that checked nothing. scripts/check-dependabot-coverage.sh fails the build if the file aims at a directory holding no manifest, or if a manifest enters the tree neither watched nor excused.

Vulnerabilities travel a separate lane: Dependabot alerts and automated security updates are repository settings rather than entries in that file, and both were switched on 2026-08-22 — so Maven and the base images do get a pull request when an advisory names one of their dependencies. One caveat survives, and it is the same CI gap: a Maven security pull request carries no build evidence at merge time, because nothing on the pull-request path compiles Java.

docs.title: The gaps, gathered once
docs.text:
Scattered today across five security pages, plus rate limits, backup/restore, and the dependency cadence in the row above. None of these are softened here — collect them for a risk register directly from this list.

Secrets & keys

  • No master-key rotation tooling: there is no re-encryption path, so changing LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY (or the connector/webhook key, LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY) leaves every secret it protects undecryptable, and losing the key makes them unrecoverable. RLS & database roles → Secrets at rest
  • The three database-role passwords (lumnik_app, lumnik_admin, lumnik_readonly) are generated per install on both deploy paths; self-host up.sh also aligns the live roles to .env on every run, which is the rotation gesture. RLS & database roles → Credentials
  • Your own ingested data (connector.t_*) and the RAG corpus (rag.chunk) are not encrypted at the application layer — plaintext PostgreSQL columns. RLS & database roles → Data at rest

Personal data & erasure

  • No DSAR export endpoint for hub data — access is real but manual, a query an integrator writes. GDPR & personal data
  • No automated hard-delete or pseudonymisation of user accounts — an archived or soft-deleted user persists in the identity schema until an operator deletes the row. GDPR & personal data
  • No deletion propagation from source systems to mirror tables — a deletion at the source does not remove the row from connector.t_*; erasure is the documented rebuild procedure. GDPR & personal data
  • No API to erase a dead-letter payload — the read surface honours the soft-delete flag everywhere, but setting it is a database operation. GDPR & personal data
  • Neither user-archive (DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id}) nor SCIM's DELETE is a GDPR erasure — both leave the row in the database until an operator removes it. SCIM deprovisioning → The /scim/v2/Users contract

Database trust boundary

  • lumnik_admin is BYPASSRLS by design — every code path using it must filter by tenant explicitly; a bug there is a cross-tenant bug RLS will not catch. RLS & database roles → What RLS does NOT protect against
  • Whoever holds the lumnik_admin credentials, or the database superuser, reads every tenant's rows regardless of RLS. RLS & database roles → What RLS does NOT protect against
  • A wrong GUC. RLS trusts app.current_tenant; the tenant resolution upstream (JWT claim → TenantContextFilter) is part of the trusted computing base — a bug there is invisible to RLS, which only enforces the policy, not how the GUC got set. RLS & database roles → What RLS does NOT protect against
  • Nothing behind the TLS edge is encrypted. The hub speaks plain HTTP internally; hub↔PostgreSQL, hub↔Ollama, and façade↔hub inside the compose/cluster network all ride the clear. TLS terminates only at the edge you put in front (the Caddy façade, your own reverse proxy, or the k8s Gateway) — securing the internal network itself is the operator's job, same as disk encryption above. RLS & database roles → Data in transit

Capacity & backup

  • Inbound rate limiting is single-node, in-memory: scale the hub to N replicas and the effective limit becomes up to N× the configured rpm — a known, deliberate trade, not an oversight. Inbound rate limits → Single-node caveat
  • No point-in-time recovery — the self-host backup is a nightly snapshot, not WAL archiving; the Helm path leans entirely on your cluster's own volume-snapshot tooling for anything beyond the PostgreSQL dump. Backup & restore → What this does NOT give you
  • .env (holding LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY) is not covered by the backup script — copy it somewhere safe separately, or a restored install cannot decrypt its own secrets. Backup & restore → Take a backup

Supply chain

  • A Maven security fix is merged on the nightly's word. Dependabot alerts and automated security updates were switched on 2026-08-22, so an advisory against a Java dependency or a container base image does open a pull request. But nothing on the pull-request path compiles or tests Java, so that pull request arrives with no build evidence: nightly-verify.yml is the first job to run it, on cron, after the merge. The three watched ecosystems — GitHub Actions, Go, the docs pin — do not have this gap; their bumps are verified by the pull request that proposes them. See the Vulnerability disclosure row above.

Edition boundary

  • BYO IdP for an actual external issuer is effectively unavailable on the open edition — not merely un-automated. JIT provisioning and the whole SCIM surface are absent entirely: they live under io.lumnik.hub.pro.*, which the -DopenEdition build profile excludes wholesale (lumnik-hub/pom.xml, alongside the Kafka connector).
  • Why: a real customer IdP normally cannot emit the optional user_id claim (it would have to know lumnik's own database primary key), so with no JitUserProvisioner on the classpath the open edition has no other way to resolve a first login.
  • Result: TenantContextFilter fails closed — 401 {"error":"no external identity resolution in this edition (user_id claim required)"}. Plan the account lifecycle, and the edition, accordingly. Bring your own IdP · SCIM deprovisioning
  • Three of the four rate-limited endpoints don't exist on the open edition either. platform-chat, user-chat and platform-search are declared on resources that live in lumnik-rag (RagChatResource, UserChatResource, RagSearchResource), which is a runtime-scope dependency only inside the closed-extensions profile (lumnik-hub/pom.xml:369-379) — on an open-edition build those endpoints, and their limits, are absent from the classpath entirely. Only view-generate (native to lumnik-hub) is enforced there. Inbound rate limits → Edition boundary

Identity & audit

  • The audit trail covers User and Secret writes plus entity reads, and stops there — with two gaps of its own. @Auditable is applied to exactly one entity; Secret is covered by three explicit call sites instead, because native SQL there bypasses Hibernate entirely:

    Piece Role Status @Auditable (lumnik-common) annotation an entity opts in with applied to User only (login, email, locked, defaultScope — User.java:23). Secret deliberately carries none — see below. AuditEntityListener @PostPersist/@PostUpdate only (AuditEntityListener.java:34,39) — records CREATE/UPDATE with the acting user (TenantContextFilter.currentUser()); skips when the tenant guard reads null (AuditEntityListener.java:48-49) fires on every Hibernate write to User, including an archive (UserResource.deactivate() → archive() → a plain field mutation, flushed as an UPDATE — archivedAt isn't a snapshotted field, so it's indistinguishable from any other edit); does not fire on SCIM-driven User writes — see below SecretResource.recordAudit() three explicit calls — create(), update() (rotate), delete() — same shape as EntityReadResource's read call: a separate admin-datasource connection, fail-soft, logged only (SecretResource.java) fires on every platform.secret write; Secret (name, description, rotatedAt, never the ciphertext or the plaintext value — pinned by a dedicated test) carries no @Auditable because production never writes it through Hibernate — an annotation implying otherwise was itself a false claim, now removed EntityReadResource.read() one explicit call after the query succeeds, recording READ with the entity name and the acting user (EntityReadResource.java:82,95-111) fires on every GET /api/entities/{name}; a refused (403/404) read is never recorded core.audit_outbox / core.audit_event drained every 2s by AuditDispatcher into the partitioned, append-only event table receives rows from the three paths above — still empty for every other entity and operation. Not uniformly transactional with the write it records — see below.

    Non-atomicity — the SecretResource paths can record a write that never happened. AuditEntityListener inserts the outbox row on the same JDBC connection as the business write, inside a savepoint (AuditEntityListener.java:118-149): the audit row and the business write commit or roll back together, so calling this leg of the trail "transactional" is accurate. SecretResource.recordAudit() does not share that property: it writes through the separate admin datasource, which runs autocommit (quarkus.datasource."admin".jdbc.transactions=disabled, application.properties:43) — deliberately, so a broken audit insert can never poison the secret write (see the method's javadoc; that separation is what a business-write-losing reentrancy bug earlier in this branch was fixed by introducing). The tradeoff is the mirror image: the audit insert commits immediately, before the surrounding @Transactional method returns and commits the secret write itself. If that later commit fails, core.audit_event is left permanently holding a CREATE/UPDATE/DELETE for a Secret write that never took effect — and the trail has no erasure path to correct it (see GDPR → The rights, in practice). EntityReadResource's read path uses the same separate-connection shape but carries none of this risk: recordRead() only runs after the read has already succeeded, so there is no later business commit for the audit row to disagree with. Separately, SecretResource.update() now checks the affected-row count before recording anything, so the narrower case — a concurrent delete landing between the existence check and the UPDATE — no longer produces a phantom audit row on its own; the cross-datasource commit-ordering gap above is the one that remains.

    Gap — SCIM-driven User writes are unaudited. ScimAuthFilter runs before TenantContextFilter and sets CurrentTenantHolder (what RLS reads) but not TenantContextFilter.CURRENT_TENANT (what AuditEntityListener's tenant guard reads) — TenantContextFilter also unconditionally clears that thread-local at the top of its own filter(), before it even checks whether the request was pre-authenticated, so setting it from ScimAuthFilter (which runs first, at AUTHENTICATION priority) would be wiped a moment later anyway. Closing this cleanly means reordering a security-sensitive filter that a dozen other call sites read (HookExecutor, ConnectorEngine, JdbcSourceResource, BffResource, ListResource, DlqAdminResource, EventOutboxService, ScimTokenResource, among others) — out of scope for a branch about wiring the existing trail. Every SCIM create, update and deactivate — including deprovisioning, the single most audit-relevant identity event there is — silently skips the listener today.

    Verified: of every @Auditable use in the codebase, exactly one sits on a production JPA @Entity — User.java:23. (Secret no longer carries it; the remaining mentions are the annotation's own declaration, javadoc prose, and @Auditable fixtures inside this branch's own tests, none of which are production entities.) An auditor asking "who changed this, and when" gets an answer for non-SCIM user-account changes, secrets and entity reads — SCIM-driven identity changes and every other entity are still a table with no rows, and there is still no read surface over the trail: querying it is a direct SQL query against core.audit_event, not an API.

  • The permission catalog is declarative metadata, not yet enforced. @RequiresPermission annotations still reference realm roles as magic strings; the per-permission catalog in roles.yaml documents the mapping but does not (yet) drive the interceptor. Roles & permissions → Conceptual model

  • Access denials are logged, not audited. PermissionInterceptor writes every denial to the application log at WARN level — SIEM can subscribe to that, but there is no structured audit-table record of who was denied what, when. Roles & permissions → Audit logging
  • The role catalog is incomplete against what is actually enforced. lm_integrator gates /api/platform/* in its entirety (PlatformApiAuthFilter) plus the view and workflow apply endpoints — but it is declared in neither shipped META-INF/roles.yaml (lumnik-hub, lumnik-rag), so it cannot appear in the roles catalog an operator reviews. An RBAC inventory taken from that catalog will be missing a role that grants real access. Roles & permissions
  • Changing the public origin orphans JIT identities. Users are keyed (idp_issuer, idp_subject); a hostname or scheme change between backup and restore (or any issuer-URL change) re-provisions every user as a new identity and can collide on the login unique constraint. Backup & restore → Known scar

docs.text: • RLS & database roles · Roles & permissions · Bring your own IdP · SCIM deprovisioning · GDPR & personal data

docs.title: Bring your own IdP
docs.text:
The hub validates any OIDC issuer generically — no Keycloak-specific code. Your IdP authenticates; lumnik provisions the user on first login (JIT) into a pre-seeded tenant.

Operator guide for plugging a customer's existing IdP (Keycloak, Okta, Entra ID, any OIDC issuer) into lumnik — enterprise onboarding without deploying a second Keycloak.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
The hub validates the Bearer token against your issuer (discovery + JWKS), reads the mandatory tenant_id claim to scope every query through PostgreSQL Row-Level Security, and — on a user's first login — creates the lumnik user, keyed on (idp_issuer, idp_subject). No password ever lives in lumnik; no user list is synced up front. Departures ride SCIM — JIT never reactivates a deactivated identity.

The crucial rule: JIT creates users, never tenants. The tenant row must pre-exist — seeded by the operator at onboarding. A token claiming a tenant_id with no matching tenant row fails the first login, by design: a tenant is an operator decision, not a side effect of someone signing in.

Edition note. JIT provisioning ships in the self-host and Helm builds this page documents, so the walkthroughs below work as written. It is absent from the separately-published open edition, which fails closed instead: a token without a user_id claim gets 401 {"error":"no external identity resolution in this edition (user_id claim required)"}. Since a real customer IdP cannot know lumnik's internal user ids, BYO IdP in practice needs a build that carries JIT.

docs.title: Prerequisites checklist
docs.text:
Before the first user logs in:

1. Seed the tenant row. A fresh install seeds tenant 1 (code='default'). Every other tenant is yours to create, run as the owner role (BYPASSRLS):

INSERT INTO identity.tenant (id, code, name, created_at, updated_at)
VALUES (42, 'acme', 'ACME Corp', now(), now())
ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;

(Or POST /api/tenants as lm_superadmin. Explicit ids below 1000 are safe — the sequence starts at 1000.)

2. Register a client in your IdP for each surface: one for lm (device flow) and — if you use the PWA — the SPA client (public + PKCE). See the SPA warning below.

3. Map the claims onto the access token:

Claim Required What it must carry aud yes Exactly lumnik-backend — the hub pins this audience; a token without it never gets past the OIDC layer (401). tenant_id yes The seeded tenant id, as an integer. groups yes The realm-role array: lm_user, lm_integrator, lm_admin, plus any scope:<tag> grants — literal lumnik role names, flat, no hierarchy (Role management). user_id no Only if your IdP knows lumnik's internal user id (the bundled realm does, and the hub seeds the row it names at install; a customer IdP normally cannot). When absent, JIT resolves the user from iss + the subject claim — the normal external-IdP posture (closed edition — see the 401 row in troubleshooting). A user_id that names no row still authenticates, but the doors that need the row answer 404. name, email no Profile fields, used only at first-login creation.

The bundled accounts occupy (tenant 1, integrator) and (tenant 11, hubadmin) on every hub; an IdP whose subject claim is a username must not reuse those logins in those tenants (uq_user_login).

The subject side of the identity key defaults to sub; override with OIDC_SUBJECT_CLAIM when your IdP has a more stable claim (see the Entra note below).

Malformed claims are rejected, never repaired — a non-integer tenant_id, an oversized issuer or subject: each fails with its own explicit 401 in the troubleshooting table. A bad profile claim never blocks a login: an over-long name is clamped, an invalid email is dropped.

docs.title: What JIT creates (and what it refuses)
docs.text:
On first login with no user_id claim, the hub creates one user row in the token's tenant: login = subject, display name from name (fallback: subject), optional email, and the (idp_issuer, idp_subject) key. Creation is race-safe with replicas > 1 — two concurrent first logins resolve to one row.

Every later login resolves the same row. A deactivated identity is refused with 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"} — JIT never reactivates or recreates; only an admin (or a SCIM re-activation flow you control) brings a user back.

docs.title: Keycloak walkthrough
docs.text:
The shipped realm (infra/keycloak/lumnik-realm.json) is the working reference — copy its mapper shapes onto your client:

Step Configuration 1. Realm roles Create lm_user, lm_integrator, lm_admin (and scope:<tag> roles if you bind métiers — Scopes). Assign them to users or groups; the hub matches names flat. 2. tenant_id mapper User Attribute mapper, user attribute tenant_id, claim tenant_id, JSON type long, on the access token. Set the attribute per user (or per group) to the seeded tenant id. 3. groups mapper User Realm Role mapper, claim name groups, multivalued, on the access token. 4. Audience mapper Audience mapper adding lumnik-backend to the access token. Every client that calls the hub needs it — see the SPA scar below. 5. lm client OIDC client with device flow enabled; point the CLI at your issuer (lm config set-context ... --oidc-issuer https://idp.example.com/realms/corp --oidc-client-id <your-client>).

docs.title: Okta / Entra ID notes
docs.text:
One layer to re-own when you swap IdPs: the bundled realm ships brute-force detection on (temporary lockout); with your own IdP, login throttling and lockout are your IdP's policies — lumnik neither sees nor throttles password attempts.

The hub needs only discovery/JWKS at the issuer URL and the claims above, so Okta and Entra work on paper. In practice, only Keycloak is exercised by the shipped rehearsal (make k8s-up-oidc-external) — neither has been run against a live hub. And because neither emits a user_id claim, first login for either rides the JIT path — mind the edition note.

  • Okta: custom claims (tenant_id, groups) and a custom audience require a custom authorization server; map groups to the lumnik role names, not Okta group ids.
  • Entra ID: sub is pairwise per app registration — stable for one app, but re-registering the app mints new subjects and orphans every JIT identity. Prefer OIDC_SUBJECT_CLAIM=oid (the tenant-stable object id). Entra's default groups claim emits group GUIDs — you need claims-mapping policy (or app roles emitted into a groups claim) to carry the literal lm_* names.
  • SAML-only IdPs (ADFS and friends): not supported by direct trust — front them with a broker (a Keycloak you or the customer operates) and point lumnik at the broker.

docs.title: Kubernetes: auth.mode=oidc-external
docs.text:
The Helm chart carries a first-class mode for this: trust the customer's issuer, deploy no Keycloak.

# deploy/helm/lumnik/values.yaml
auth:
  mode: oidc-external

oidc:
  external:
    issuerUrl: "https://idp.customer.com/realms/corp"   # discovery/JWKS
    tokenIssuer: ""   # token `iss` to validate; defaults to issuerUrl.
                      # Set ONLY when it differs (a port-forward split on kind).

The chart fails fast: a typo'd auth.mode aborts helm install (instead of silently pointing the hub at a Keycloak that was never deployed), and oidc-external with an empty issuerUrl refuses to render. Both oidc and oidc-external run the hub on %prod (dev-bypass OFF); only where the issuer points differs.

To rehearse the whole shape locally — a stand-in "customer IdP" in its own namespace, the hub trusting it, the release provably Keycloak-free:

make k8s-up-oidc-external

A real customer IdP is then an issuerUrl swap — zero chart change, zero hub code change. Leave tokenIssuer empty in real deployments (the split exists only for the kind port-forward).

docs.title: The PWA client (lumnik-spa)
docs.text: ⚠️ The audience-mapper scar. The hub pins aud: lumnik-backend on every access token — and a freshly-created SPA client emits no audience by default. The bundled lumnik-spa client learned this live: without the audience mapper, every PWA call is a 401 while lm works fine. When you register the SPA client in the customer IdP: public client + PKCE (S256), redirect URI https://<hub-origin>/app/*, and the audience mapper on the access token. Full PWA auth lifecycle: the métier PWA.

docs.title: The issuer is part of the identity
docs.text: ⚠️ Changing the issuer URL orphans JIT identities. Users are keyed (idp_issuer, idp_subject). Move the origin — plain-http to TLS, hostname change, issuer path change — and the same human becomes a new identity, whose first login then collides with the old row's login (uq_user_login, surfaced as an explicit error). Pick the public origin once, early, before the first real login. If you must move: migrate identity.app_user.idp_issuer deliberately, or accept re-provisioning by clearing the old-issuer users. Details: upgrade and backup/restore.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix 401 {"error":"missing or invalid tenant_id claim"} No tenant_id on the access token, or a non-integer value (a fractional id is rejected, never truncated) Add/fix the tenant_id mapper (JSON type long, access token) 401 with no lumnik error body Token rejected by the OIDC layer: wrong/missing aud: lumnik-backend, or iss ≠ the configured token issuer Add the audience mapper; check issuerUrl/tokenIssuer match the token's iss 401 {"error":"missing subject/issuer claim"} No user_id claim and the subject claim is absent Check OIDC_SUBJECT_CLAIM names a claim the IdP actually emits 401 {"error":"no external identity resolution in this edition (user_id claim required)"} No user_id claim, and the running build is the open-source edition (no JIT) Deploy the default self-host/Helm build (JIT ships there) 401 {"error":"subject/issuer claim too long"} iss or subject exceeds 255 chars — rejected, never truncated: truncating the key would change the identity Use a shorter stable claim (e.g. Entra oid) 404 {"error":"no user record on this hub for user_id N"} on lm scope / …/users/me/scope The IdP emits a user_id that names no hub row Point it at an existing hub row id, or drop it so JIT resolves the user (401 row above: not in the open edition) First login 500, logs show fk_user_tenant Tenant row not seeded — JIT creates users, never tenants Seed the tenant (checklist above), retry 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"} Identity exists but was deactivated (e.g. SCIM departure) Reactivate via admin — JIT never resurrects 403 on every endpoint despite valid login groups claim missing or carrying IdP-native names instead of lm_* Map realm roles into groups as literal lumnik role names Login error after moving to TLS / new hostname Issuer change orphaned the JIT identity; new row collides on uq_user_login Migrate idp_issuer on existing rows (scar box above)

docs.title: GDPR & personal data
docs.text:
Where personal data can live in a lumnik installation, what erasure actually does today, and — named rather than hidden — the handful of things GDPR compliance would still need that are not built yet.

lumnik is self-hosted software, not a service: it runs on your infrastructure, and no data ever reaches a lumnik cloud — there isn't one. You remain the controller (or processor) of the data it touches; this page is not legal advice. It is an engineering map: where personal data can live inside a lumnik installation, which controls exist — each claim backed by shipped code — and what is not built yet.

docs.title: The posture, in three sentences
docs.text:
• Nothing leaves your infrastructure by default. Chat and embeddings run on a local model runtime (Ollama); the questions your users ask and the data chunks that ground the answers travel to localhost, not to an API on the internet. Switching to a cloud LLM provider is possible, but it is an explicit configuration you make — and from that moment those chunks and questions are sent to that provider.
  • lumnik is a read-only mirror. Ingestion reads your source systems and never writes back; the source remains the system of record. Ask-to-SQL executes under a dedicated read-only database role, behind five honesty guards that include a leak guard refusing any query outside the user's granted scope.
  • Isolation is enforced in the database itself. Every tenant's rows are separated by PostgreSQL row-level security (RLS & database roles), and chat, search and entity reads are additionally scope-bound per métier.

docs.title: Where personal data can live
docs.text: Store What lands there Lifecycle identity schema lumnik user accounts: login, display name, email Archive / soft-delete lifecycle — see below connector.t_* mirror tables Whatever your sources contain (customers, orders…) Rows are upserted by content hash; a deletion at the source does not propagate — see Erasure rag.chunk corpus Text chunks + embeddings derived from ingested rows Append-and-dedup at ingestion (row_hash): a changed source row adds a new chunk and the old one stays; a row deleted at the source keeps its chunk. Erasure rides the connector: deleting it cascades to every chunk it produced (fk_chunk_connector, pinned by an integration test under enforced RLS). Only the platform corpus (source: system) is replaced wholesale, at boot and on reindex Dead letters The raw payload of rows that failed mapping (kept on purpose, for diagnosis) Every read surface excludes soft-deleted rows; nothing sets that flag via API today — see Not built Event outbox entity name, a key hash, the operation — no row content Purged daily once older than the retention window (lumnik.events.retention-days, default 30 days) and consumed by every registered consumer Audit trail (core.audit_event) Narrow, but real: User writes (non-SCIM), Secret writes (metadata only — never a value), view/workflow applies (with the manifest's SHA-256), and entity READs — each row with the acting user. How it is written, and the two gaps Populated for those paths; empty for everything else; append-only, bounded by time: the nightly purge deletes rows older than LUMNIK_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 365 days; 0 = keep forever, an explicit choice) — no per-row erasure, see Erasure Webhook deliveries (egress) The values of row columns a kind: Process message template references — sent in clear to the webhook target the tenant configured (n8n, Make, your endpoint) Leaves lumnik entirely; retention is the receiving system's. The delivery history row lumnik keeps stores status and attempts Keycloak Its own user store (credentials, sessions) Your realm, your policies Backups Whatever you back up Yours entirely

docs.title: How the audit trail is written
docs.text:
Two write paths plus reads, narrowly:

  • User writes (login, email, locked, defaultScope) via @Auditable + AuditEntityListener (@PostPersist/@PostUpdate).
  • Secret writes (name, description, rotatedAt — never the ciphertext or the plaintext value) via three explicit calls in SecretResource (create, rotate, delete): Secret carries no @Auditable because its writes go through native SQL to keep pgp_sym_encrypt in PostgreSQL, which bypasses Hibernate entirely — the listener could never have fired on it.
  • View / workflow applies (SavedView, WorkflowManifest): actor, name, scope, and the manifest's SHA-256 — recorded explicitly for the same reason: their stores write raw JDBC.
  • READ events from GET /api/entities/{name}, recorded explicitly in EntityReadResource.read().

Each row carries the acting user (TenantContextFilter.currentUser()). The two gaps:

  • Gap 1 — archiving a user (DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id}) is recorded, but only as an ordinary UPDATE: archivedAt isn't a snapshotted field, so it looks like any other edit.
  • Gap 2 — SCIM-driven User writes (create, update, deprovision) are not recorded at all — see Not built below.

docs.title: The rights, in practice
docs.text:
Access & portability. Entity reads (GET /api/entities/{name}) and read-only SQL give structured access to everything lumnik holds about a person. There is no one-click DSAR export — assembling an answer is a query your integrator writes, not a button.

Rectification. Fix the data in the source system; the mirror follows on the next run. The RAG corpus gains a chunk for the corrected row on that same run — but ingestion is append-and-dedup, so the chunk carrying the old value stays until the connector is deleted and re-ingested (the erasure gesture below). When a rectification must also purge the wrong value from the corpus, use that gesture. lumnik deliberately offers no way to edit ingested rows — a mirror that can be edited stops being evidence of what the source said.

Erasure splits into two very different cases:

  • A person in your data (a customer row in a mirror table): erase them in the source system first — it is the system of record. Then, because deletions do not propagate, rebuild the mirror: delete the connector and re-ingest. lm connector delete purges its dynamic tables and registry rows, and the same delete cascades to every RAG chunk that connector produced (fk_chunk_connector ON DELETE CASCADE — proven by an integration test under enforced RLS), so the erased row's text and embeddings die with it. Removing rows from connector.t_* by hand is not enough: ingestion appends chunks with hash-dedup and nothing re-indexes ingested data (reindex rebuilds only the platform corpus), so a hand-deleted row's chunk would survive until the connector itself is deleted.
  • A lumnik user account: DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id} archives the user (archived_at); SCIM DELETE soft-deletes it (deleted_at) — two distinct states, see SCIM deprovisioning for why they differ. Either way the next login attempt is refused with 403 and the account drops out of listings; a soft-deleted row is additionally treated as absent by payload-bearing surfaces like the dead-letter queue. What neither state is: a deletion — the row remains in the database until an operator removes it, see below. Neither state removes anything from the audit trail either. A non-SCIM archive adds to it: core.audit_event snapshots the login/email at the moment they were last recorded (see the table above) into an append-only log with no per-row erasure tooling — archiving, soft-deleting, or hand-deleting the identity row does not remove or redact the copies already written to audit_event. What bounds those copies is time: the nightly retention purge deletes audit rows older than LUMNIK_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 365 days; 0 keeps them forever, as an explicit operator choice).

docs.title: Not built yet, recorded not hidden
docs.text:
The asymmetry-of-harm rule this product applies to its chat — abstain rather than answer confidently wrong — applies to this page too. The following do not exist today:

  • No automated hard-delete or pseudonymisation of user accounts. An archived or soft-deleted user persists in the identity schema until an operator deletes the row in the database. (An earlier revision of the SCIM page described a nightly purge and a gdpr/erase endpoint; neither was ever built — that page has been corrected.)
  • No DSAR export endpoint for hub data. Access is real but manual (queries over the entity and SQL surfaces).
  • No deletion propagation from source systems to mirror tables. Erasure of ingested data is the rebuild procedure described above.
  • No API to erase a dead-letter payload. The read seam already honours the soft-delete flag everywhere; setting it is a database operation.
  • The audit trail covers User and Secret writes plus entity reads, not the whole system — and has two gaps of its own. core.audit_event records User writes via @Auditable + AuditEntityListener, Secret writes via three explicit calls in SecretResource (native SQL there bypasses Hibernate, so Secret carries no @Auditable), and GET /api/entities/{name} reads — see the table above. No other entity is covered. Archiving a user IS recorded, but only as an ordinary UPDATE (archivedAt is not a snapshotted field), so it is indistinguishable from any other edit. SCIM-driven User writes are not recorded at all: ScimAuthFilter sets the tenant RLS reads (CurrentTenantHolder) but not the separate thread-local the listener's tenant guard checks (TenantContextFilter.CURRENT_TENANT), so every SCIM create/update/deactivate — including deprovisioning, the single most audit-relevant identity event there is — silently skips the listener. This is a known, left-as-is gap: closing it means reordering a security-sensitive auth filter that a dozen other call sites depend on, for a branch about wiring the trail, not about touching that filter. There is also still no read surface over the trail — an auditor queries core.audit_event directly, the same as before, and once a row lands there it cannot be erased or redacted (see Erasure above). Accountability for anything outside these paths is, today, whatever your database and reverse proxy log.

If one of these gaps blocks a real obligation you have, say so — they are unbuilt because no deployment has needed them yet, not because they are hard.

docs.title: Tenants, users & scopes — the admin gestures
docs.text:
Identity lives in Keycloak, not in lumnik: creating a human, giving them roles, granting a métier scope are Keycloak-console gestures, and the hub follows the JWT. This page walks each gesture in the bundled console — no Keycloak manual required (the official docs are for the hyper-curious).

The model in four lines. The hub trusts three JWT claims: tenant_id (which tenant), user_id (which row), and the realm roles (lm_* for permissions, scope:* for métier fences). The bundled realm lumnik already carries the protocol mappers that turn the user attributes tenant_id / user_id into those claims — you only set attributes and roles on users. A user with a user_id is bound to that row directly and never provisioned — the bundled integrator (user_id=1) has its row seeded at install, and a user_id that names no row still authenticates but the doors that need the row (default scope) answer 404. Outside the open edition, a user without one is JIT-provisioned at first login; SCIM deprovisions it (SCIM).

Console: http://localhost:8180 → realm lumnik (admin credentials from your .env). The realm ships with brute-force detection on (temporary lockout at Keycloak's defaults — tune it under Realm settings → Security defenses). The console is local-only by design — the compose pins Keycloak to 127.0.0.1 and the TLS façade proxies only /realms/* (the OIDC endpoints), never the admin console. On a remote host, reach it through an SSH tunnel (reach the hub from another machine).

docs.title: Add a user
docs.text:
1. Users → Add user — username, email; Create.
  2. Credentials tab → set a password (or let the IdP federation handle it).
  3. Attributes tab → add tenant_id = the tenant's numeric id.
  4. Role mapping tab → Assign role → lm_user (plus any scope:* roles — see below).

Result (outside the open edition): the first login JIT-creates the hub row in that tenant — nothing to do on the lumnik side. Open edition: there is no JIT — also add a user_id attribute pointing at an existing hub user row (POST /api/tenants/{tid}/users, lm_admin); a JWT without it is refused 401.

docs.title: Grant (or revoke) a métier scope
docs.text:
Scope roles are created on demand — the shipped realm has none, because zero scope:* roles means unscoped, tenant-wide.

  1. Realm roles → Create role — name it scope:ventes (the tag your manifests use in spec.scope).
  2. Users → the user → Role mapping → Assign role → scope:ventes.

Result: from their next token, the user is bound: chat, search, views, entity reads answer only inside granted scopes — anything else refuses with 403 {"error":"scope not granted"} (Scopes). Revoking works the same gesture in reverse; removing their last scope role makes them tenant-wide again.

docs.title: Make someone admin, integrator, superadmin
docs.text:
Same Role mapping gesture; what each unlocks:

Role Unlocks lm_user the app surface — chat, views, inbox, PWA lm_admin tenant administration — integrations, notification rules, business lists lm_integrator the /api/platform/* surface lm drives — connectors, manifests, runs lm_superadmin cross-tenant: tenant CRUD and impersonation

Roles are separate, not ranked — an integrator is not automatically an admin (role management).

docs.title: Onboard a new tenant
docs.text:
1. Create the tenant row (superadmin): 
    TOKEN=$(awk '/^ *access:/ {print $2; exit}' ~/.lm/config.yaml)
curl -s -X POST https://your-hub.example.com/api/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"code": "ACME", "name": "Acme Corp"}'    # both required; note the returned id
  2. In Keycloak, create its first admin (gesture above) with tenant_id = the returned id and roles lm_user + lm_admin.

Result: that admin's first login lands in the new tenant; RLS fences every read and write to it from the first request.

docs.title: Offboard someone
docs.text: active: false from your IdP via SCIM (not on the open edition) archives the user — tokens are refused from the next request. Departure of the integrator has its own checklist: offboarding.

docs.title: One surface to not misread
docs.text: POST /api/tenants/{tid}/users creates a hub row, not a login — it carries no IdP identity, so no one can authenticate as it (outside the open edition JIT creates rows by itself; on the open edition the row is what a user_id attribute points at). Treat the users API as the mirror it is, not as an onboarding path.

docs.text:

  • Bring your own IdP — the same claims from your enterprise SSO
  • SCIM · Offboarding · Scopes

docs.title: Offboarding the integrator
docs.text: SCIM covers the departure of a métier user. This page covers the other departure every RSSI documents: the integrator/consultant whose mission ends — what they could touch, and the last-day checklist.

docs.title: The access footprint
docs.text:
What an integrator typically held during the mission:

Access What it opens Where it lives A realm account with lm_integrator the platform surface behind the integrator gate — connectors, runs, secrets metadata, discovery — plus views/apply and workflows/apply; many admin endpoints stack lm_admin/lm_superadmin on top (roles) your IdP / the bundled realm The lm CLI session whatever the roles above open, from their workstation tokens in ~/.lm/config.yaml on their machine The .env of the install the master keys (LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY, LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY), Postgres and Keycloak admin passwords the server they installed Database credentials lumnik_admin is BYPASSRLS — per-install generated; rotate by putting new values in .env and re-running up.sh (credentials) anyone who read the departing integrator's .env SCIM tokens (if minted) the /scim/v2/* provisioning surface revocable, effect immediate

docs.title: The clock, on the bundled realm
docs.text:
• Access tokens live 1 hour; the refresh chain dies at the latest 24 hours after login (accessTokenLifespan: 3600, ssoSessionMaxLifespan: 86400; Keycloak's default idle timeout kills an unused chain in ~30 minutes — your own IdP may differ).
  • Archiving the account denies the very next request, even with a still-valid token — both token shapes (SCIM → deactivate). You do not wait for expiry.

docs.title: The last-day checklist
docs.text:
1. Archive or disable the account in the IdP (or active: false via SCIM). Effect: next request denied. On the bundled realm: Keycloak admin console at http://localhost:8180 (admin credentials = KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD in the install's .env), realm lumnik → Users → the account → Enabled: off — Keycloak has no "archive" button; disabling is the gesture. Removing just the lm_integrator role also works but leaves a dormant account.
  2. Revoke any SCIM tokens they minted: DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens/{id} — immediate (token lifecycle). Needs an lm_admin of the same tenant — check before the last day that the departing consultant was not the only one.
  3. Rotate what can be rotated — as a planned maintenance window, not a 5 p.m. gesture: rotating the Postgres role passwords at the database breaks the running hub until the datasource env is hand-edited and the stack restarted (the passwords are not yet externally configurable — the defaults caveat); the Keycloak admin password rotates freely. The master keys cannot be rotated in place (the warning); the nuclear option — a new key plus re-entering every stored secret by hand — exists, and for a contentious departure may be the decision to write down.
  4. Their workstation is best-effort: you cannot remotely wipe ~/.lm/config.yaml, but steps 1–2 bound it — on the bundled realm the tokens it holds die within the hour, the refresh chain within the day, and every request meanwhile is denied at the filter.
  5. Host access is your infrastructure's offboarding, not lumnik's — SSH keys in authorized_keys, VPN, sudo on the server they installed. This page cannot revoke it; your IT offboarding must. Named here so nobody stops at step 4 believing the job done.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text: There is no product surface listing "everything user X can reach" or their active sessions — the checklist above is the procedure. The checklist also only revokes what they could reach: what they left behind — connectors, mappings, and above all .kts hooks, which are code the hub keeps executing after they leave — stays running. Reviewing it is your change management; know that it is there. And as long as the Postgres role passwords ship at defaults, rotating them (with the maintenance-window caveat of step 3) remains the step that most deserves to actually happen.

docs.title: Row-Level Security & database roles
docs.text:
Every tenant's rows are isolated by PostgreSQL Row-Level Security, not by application code — the request-path database role cannot bypass it.

The first question a security reviewer asks of a multi-tenant hub: what stops tenant A from reading tenant B's rows? In lumnik the answer is PostgreSQL itself — every tenanted table carries a Row-Level Security policy, and the application connects as a role that cannot bypass it.

docs.title: The three database roles
docs.text:
Created outside Flyway by infra/postgres/init/01-roles.sh (superuser context — the migration user intentionally lacks CREATEROLE):

Role Privileges Purpose lumnik_app SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on tables, USAGE/SELECT/UPDATE on sequences (via ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES from lumnik_admin). Subject to RLS. The default datasource — every request-path query. lumnik_admin LOGIN + BYPASSRLS. Owns every table (Flyway runs as it; dynamic connector tables are created through the admin datasource too). Migrations and deliberate cross-tenant work: GDPR purge, dynamic-table DDL, secret resolution, the workflow dormancy sweep. JTA enlistment is disabled on this datasource (application.properties) so it is never picked up by accident inside a request transaction. lumnik_readonly SELECT only, default_transaction_read_only = on, USAGE on schema connector (connector/V15__schema_card_and_readonly.sql + per-table grants from the dynamic writers). Subject to RLS. The physical firewall under LLM-generated SQL: ask-to-SQL and kind:View render/detail run only through this datasource.

lumnik_app owns nothing — table ownership sits with lumnik_admin, so the owner-bypasses-own-RLS rule of PostgreSQL never applies to the request path.

flowchart LR
  req["request path — JWT"] --> app["lumnik_app<br/>RLS enforced"]
  llm["LLM-generated SQL —<br/>ask · view render"] --> ro["lumnik_readonly<br/>RLS · read-only ·<br/>empty search_path"]
  ops["migrations · dynamic DDL ·<br/>purge · dormancy sweep"] --> adm["lumnik_admin<br/>BYPASSRLS · owns the tables"]
  app -->|"SET LOCAL tenant"| t[("tenant-stamped<br/>tables")]
  ro -->|"SET LOCAL tenant"| t
  adm -->|"deliberate cross-tenant"| t

docs.title: How a query gets its tenant
docs.text:
The policy predicate reads a transaction-local GUC, app.current_tenant:

  • Default datasource — TenantConnectionInterceptor (an Agroal pool interceptor) issues SET LOCAL app.current_tenant = '<id>' once per JTA transaction, from the tenant resolved off the JWT. SET LOCAL dies with the transaction — nothing leaks onto the pooled connection. Background/system work sets the sentinel '0'; a request claiming tenant <= 0 is rejected (sentinel-spoofing guard, fail closed).
  • Readonly datasource — TenantRlsScope.applyTo(connection, tenantId) (one shared entry point) marks the connection read-only, sets the GUC, and empties search_path so a bare table name cannot sidestep the schema-qualified leak guard.

docs.title: The policy shape
docs.text:
Since core/V21__rls_tenant_nullif_guard.sql, every statically migrated tenant policy reads:

USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant', true), '')::bigint)

No tenant set (or set to '') → the predicate is NULL → zero rows, not an error and never all rows. (Before V21, an empty GUC crashed the query with 22P02; the guard made the failure mode "no data" instead.) System-shared tables (core.event_outbox, connector.* run bookkeeping — V4, V22, V24) additionally accept the '0' sentinel.

Dynamically created connector tables (connector.t_*, ext.*, mapping-target schemas) get the same guarded policy at creation time (DynamicTableWriter / HybridJsonbWriter), and core/V31__rls_dynamic_tables_nullif_guard.sql healed every dynamic table created before the guard — surgically, by predicate shape, leaving the '0'-sentinel system policies untouched.

Original policies: core/V2__rls_policies.sql, identity/V6__rls_policies.sql.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text: Each datasource's credentials are env-overridable (application.properties): LUMNIK_APP_DB_USERNAME / LUMNIK_APP_DB_PASSWORD, LUMNIK_ADMIN_DB_USERNAME / LUMNIK_ADMIN_DB_PASSWORD, LUMNIK_READONLY_DB_USERNAME / LUMNIK_READONLY_DB_PASSWORD; all three share one DB_URL. Both deploy paths generate all three per install: self-host up.sh writes them into .env and aligns the live roles to .env on every run — so rotation is one gesture: put a new value in .env, re-run up.sh. The Helm path injects them through the release Secret (secrets.appDbPassword / adminDbPassword / readonlyDbPassword), consumed by the init script at first boot and by the hub's datasources at every boot; on a cluster with an existing data volume, rotate at the database (ALTER ROLE … PASSWORD) and upgrade with the matching values. Installs older than this mechanism rotate automatically the first time up.sh runs with the new keys in .env.

docs.title: What RLS does NOT protect against
docs.text:
• The admin datasource. lumnik_admin is BYPASSRLS by design; every code path using it must filter explicitly (WHERE tenant_id = ? — e.g. PgcryptoSecretResolver). A bug there is a cross-tenant bug RLS will not catch.
  • The database superuser, or anyone holding the lumnik_admin credentials.
  • A wrong GUC. RLS trusts app.current_tenant; the tenant resolution upstream (JWT claim → TenantContextFilter) is part of the trusted computing base.

docs.title: Secrets at rest: the master key
docs.text:
One key. No rotation. No recovery.

Back up LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY somewhere safe, today — it is not in the backup script. Change it and every stored secret becomes undecryptable. Lose it and they are unrecoverable. There is no re-encryption tooling, so a key change means re-entering every secret by hand.

Tenant secrets are encrypted in the database with pgcrypto — AES-256, under one symmetric master key.

What is encrypted tenant secrets — platform.secret (platform/V14__platform_secret.sql) How pgcrypto pgp_sym_encrypt, AES-256 The key lumnik.secret.master-key, injected via env LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY Who creates it the self-host and k8s installers, openssl rand -base64 32, at install time (into .env / a Helm secret) Refuses to boot MasterKeyValidator, on a blank, placeholder, or short (< 16 chars) key

Rotating one secret's value — supported. Re-apply it; rotated_at is stamped.

Rotating the master key — not supported today. See the warning above.

A second key behaves identically. LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY (lumnik.crypto.secret-key, SecretCipher) covers connector and webhook credentials, with the same no-rotation posture and the same AES-256. Credentials stored by builds that predate the AES-256 switch were written AES-128; they stay readable (the algorithm travels in the PGP header) and move to AES-256 the next time the credential is re-saved.

docs.title: Data at rest: what is encrypted, and what is not
docs.text:
Your own ingested data is not encrypted at the application layer. Encryption there is scoped to two stores only — tenant secrets and connector/webhook credentials, the same master-key-protected stores described above.

DynamicTableWriter builds connector.t_* with plain CREATE TABLE DDL, no cipher column in sight, and RagWriter inserts chunk text and embeddings into rag.chunk the same way. Whatever your source systems hold — names, emails, order history, anything — lands in PostgreSQL as plaintext columns, readable to anyone who can query the database directly (the lumnik_admin/superuser caveat above applies here too).

That is a defensible posture for self-hosted software the customer's own infrastructure runs, not an oversight: volume/disk encryption and backup encryption are the operator's layer, same as for any other database. Encrypt the PostgreSQL volume and the backup artifacts at the infrastructure level if your data classification requires it — lumnik does not do that for you, and does not claim to.

docs.title: Data in transit: where TLS stops
docs.text:
The hub itself speaks plain HTTP: quarkus.http.port=8080 (lumnik-hub/src/main/resources/application.properties:2), with no quarkus.http.ssl.* setting anywhere in that file — there is no https:// origin baked into the application. Both shipped deploy paths put something in front of it:

  • Self-host — the optional TLS façade (deploy/tls/Caddyfile) terminates HTTPS at $LUMNIK_TLS_HOST and reverse-proxies to hub:8080 and keycloak:8180 over the compose's internal Docker network: browser↔façade is HTTPS, façade↔hub and façade↔Keycloak are plain HTTP inside the container network. Skip the façade and the hub answers in the clear on whatever you exposed port 8080 to.
  • Kubernetes — the Gateway resource (deploy/helm/lumnik/templates/gateway.yaml:11-20) terminates TLS from a secret (gateway.tlsSecretName, self-signed by up.sh unless you supply your own); the hop from the Gateway to the hub pod is, same as self-host, plain HTTP inside the cluster network.

Nothing behind the TLS edge is encrypted. TLS terminates at whichever edge you put in front of the stack — the Caddy façade, your own reverse proxy, or the k8s Gateway. Everything behind that edge — hub↔PostgreSQL, hub↔Ollama, façade↔hub — rides your internal network in the clear.

Neither hub↔PostgreSQL nor hub↔Ollama is configured for TLS: the JDBC URLs (application.properties:10-11, %dev/%prod) carry no sslmode parameter, and OLLAMA_BASE_URL defaults to http://localhost:11434 (lumnik-llm-langchain/src/main/resources/application.properties:5) — plain HTTP, container-to-container or container-to-host.

Securing that internal network (a private VPC/VLAN, no public exposure of the DB/Ollama ports) is the operator's job, same as the disk encryption above. No new promise here either.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Hub refuses to boot: lumnik.secret.master-key is not set / is still the placeholder / is too short (< 16 chars) MasterKeyValidator rejects a blank, placeholder, or short LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY before the app starts Generate a real key (openssl rand -base64 32) and export it as LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY A secret fails to resolve at runtime: SecretResolver failed for name=… tenant=… LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY was changed or lost since the secret was encrypted — pgp_sym_decrypt cannot open it with the current key Restore the original key from backup; there is no re-encryption path (see Secrets at rest) A query through lumnik_app/lumnik_readonly returns zero rows, though lumnik_admin/psql shows the data is there app.current_tenant was never set on that connection (a manual psql session, or code that skipped the normal request/readonly path) — the RLS predicate evaluates to NULL, not an error Confirm the query went through TenantConnectionInterceptor or TenantRlsScope, not a raw connection

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Roles & permissions — the application-layer RBAC above this.
  • Scopes — the métier boundary layered on top of tenant isolation.

docs.title: Role management
docs.text:
Four lm_* realm roles gate which surfaces a user can reach; scope:<tag> grants narrow which métier's data those surfaces show — flat matching, no hierarchy, so every role a user needs must be granted explicitly.

Operator guide for the lumnik RBAC catalog.

docs.title: Conceptual model
docs.text:
Everything a user may do rides in on their Keycloak realm roles — four lm_* roles that open surfaces, plus any number of scope:<tag> grants that limit which métier's data those surfaces show:

flowchart LR
  u["lm_user"] --> s1["business reads —<br/>entities · views · chat"]
  i["lm_integrator"] --> s2["/api/platform/* —<br/>connectors · ingestion"]
  a["lm_admin"] --> s3["tenant administration"]
  sa["lm_superadmin"] --> s4["platform-wide —<br/>tenant list · impersonation"]
  sc["scope:achat · scope:stock …"] -.->|"limits WHICH métier's data,<br/>inside what a role opened"| s1
Role Opens lm_user the business read surfaces — /api/entities/*, views, chat lm_integrator connectors and ingestion — the /api/platform/* surface lm_admin tenant administration lm_superadmin platform-wide: tenant list + impersonation — the only role with wildcard: true

No hierarchy. The interceptor matches role names flat — lm_admin does not imply lm_user. Grant every role a user needs explicitly. The self-host demo realm does: integrator carries integrator+admin+user, hubadmin admin+user+superadmin (the native-claims k8s variant grants hubadmin only lm_admin).

Scope grants are realm roles too, by naming convention: scope:<tag> (e.g. scope:achat). They are opt-in — a user with none is unscoped (tenant-wide), one or more binds them to exactly those métiers. No entry in roles.yaml is needed; see Scopes.

Beneath the roles sits a second layer: permissions, declared per module in META-INF/module-manifest.yaml (e.g. repair.read, request.manage). The role→permission mapping lives in lumnik-hub/src/main/resources/META-INF/roles.yaml and is exposed in the admin console under Rôles (/admin/{tid}/roles).

Current enforcement model

@RequiresPermission(...) annotations on REST resources still reference realm roles as magic strings (e.g. @RequiresPermission("lm_admin")). The permission catalog is declarative metadata — it documents the mapping but does not (yet) drive the interceptor. A future plan will resolve permissions through RoleRegistry.

docs.title: Adding a new role
docs.text:
1. Edit lumnik-hub/src/main/resources/META-INF/roles.yaml and add the role under roles:.
  2. Declare the role in the Keycloak realm lumnik (or your environment's equivalent).
  3. Restart the platform. Boot logs should show Roles loaded: N roles from M roles.yaml files.
  4. Visit /admin/{tid}/roles and confirm the new role appears.

If the platform refuses to start with a message like Role 'lm_foo' references unknown permission 'bar.baz', either remove the permission from the role grant or add it to the relevant module's module-manifest.yaml.

docs.title: Adding a new permission
docs.text:
1. Add the permission id to the relevant module-manifest.yaml: 
    permissions:
  - id: invoice.export
    label:
      en: "Export invoices"
      fr: "Exporter les factures"
  2. Grant the permission to the roles that should have it by adding the id under roles.yaml → roles[].permissions.
  3. Restart the platform. If the permission is not yet granted by any role, you will see a WARN log: Orphan permissions (declared by modules, granted by no role): [invoice.export].
  4. Use the permission id in a @RequiresPermission annotation. Today, until the interceptor refactor lands, this still resolves against realm roles — so the annotation value must remain the realm role name (lm_admin etc.). The permission catalog is only metadata at this stage (Conceptual model → current enforcement model).

docs.title: Dev-bypass
docs.text:
Setting lumnik.security.dev-bypass=true in application.properties (or via the env var LUMNIK_SECURITY_DEV_BYPASS=true) injects the three realm roles {lm_superadmin, lm_admin, lm_user} into every request. This is enabled by default in %dev and %test profiles.

To test access refusals locally, set the flag to false and provide a valid JWT with the required roles in the groups claim. There is no header that overrides roles — dev-bypass grants the fixed set above (identity comes from X-Tenant-ID / X-User-ID headers); in production the roles always come from the JWT.

docs.title: The entity-read scope gate
docs.text:
Realm roles answer may this user call the endpoint; scope grants answer which métier's data may they see there. A scope-bound user (one or more scope:<tag> realm roles) hitting a read surface outside their granted set gets the uniform refusal:

403 {"error":"scope not granted"}

The check is ScopeGrants.allowsAny(...) (lumnik-common) against the scope tags on the resource — e.g. EntityReadResource refuses GET /api/entities/{name} when the entity manifest's scopes don't intersect the user's grants. The same gate covers saved-view discovery, view render/detail/generate, and chat.

Unscoped users (no scope:* role) pass everything — the boundary is opt-in. Full semantics: Scopes → Binding users to scopes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
These answers come from different gates:

Symptom Cause Fix 403 with an empty body PermissionInterceptor — the caller's roles include none of the endpoint's @RequiresPermission(...) values (e.g. /api/views/apply, /api/workflows/apply both require lm_integrator this way) Grant the missing role; check the endpoint's @RequiresPermission value 403 {"error":"scope not granted"} The métier-scope gate (above) — the caller has one or more scope:<tag> roles but none intersect the resource's scopes Grant the missing scope:<tag>, or remove all scope roles to go unscoped (The entity-read scope gate) 403 plain text missing role lm_integrator PlatformApiAuthFilter gates every /api/platform/* path directly, ahead of any @RequiresPermission the resource itself declares Grant lm_integrator; this is a separate gate from the empty-body case above — same missing role, different mechanism 404 {"error":"no user record on this hub for user_id N"} on lm scope The login's user_id attribute names a hub user row that does not exist (the bundled accounts are seeded at install) Point the attribute at an existing row's id, or drop it so first login creates the row (outside the open edition) — BYO IdP No 403 at all, even for an obviously wrong role, in dev/test lumnik.security.dev-bypass=true (default in %dev/%test) injects the fixed set {lm_superadmin, lm_admin, lm_user} on every request Set it false and supply a real JWT to test refusals (Dev-bypass)

docs.title: Release security checklist
docs.text:
Before each release, walk through the catalog at /admin/{tid}/roles and confirm:

  • The list of roles matches what is declared in Keycloak.
  • Only lm_superadmin carries the wildcard: true flag.
  • No permission is declared by a module without being granted by at least one role (the boot log will warn — investigate each orphan).
  • Every @RequiresPermission annotation in the codebase uses a role id present in roles.yaml: 
    grep -rn '@RequiresPermission' lumnik-*/src/main/java

This item fails today: lm_integrator

lm_integrator is used directly by @RequiresPermission("lm_integrator") (WorkflowApplyResource.java:35, ViewApplyResource.java:30) and by PlatformApiAuthFilter for every /api/platform/* path, but it is declared in neither roles.yaml (checked: lumnik-hub, lumnik-rag) — it is a Keycloak realm role (infra/keycloak/lumnik-realm.json) with no entry in the RBAC catalog, and will not appear at /admin/{tid}/roles.

docs.title: Audit logging
docs.text: PermissionInterceptor (in io.lumnik.hub.security) logs every access denial at WARN level with the required roles, the caller's roles, and the method name. SIEM consumers should subscribe to these log lines for security monitoring. The interceptor does not currently write to a structured audit table — that is on the roadmap.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• The role → permission mapping: lumnik-hub/src/main/resources/META-INF/roles.yaml
  • The bundled demo realm (roles + users): infra/keycloak/lumnik-realm.json
  • The database layer beneath RBAC: RLS & database roles

docs.title: SCIM deprovisioning
docs.text:
Not in the open edition. The entire /scim/v2/* surface and its token-management endpoints live under io.lumnik.hub.pro.scim, excluded from the published open-source edition; the self-host and Helm builds this page documents carry it by default.

Operator guide for wiring departures from your IdP (Okta, Microsoft Entra ID, Keycloak) into lumnik over SCIM 2.0.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
Arrival is automatic: a user who logs in through your IdP is JIT-provisioned on first login (see BYO IdP). Departure is not — the IdP will happily keep issuing tokens until the account is disabled there, and lumnik would keep honouring them. SCIM is the departure side: your IdP pushes active: false the moment an account is deactivated, lumnik archives the user, and the very next request is denied — even if a still-valid token is in flight. That closed loop (arrival ↔ departure) is what an access-review auditor asks to see.

The integrator's departure is a different checklist — Offboarding the integrator.

docs.title: The auth model
docs.text:
SCIM requests do not carry user JWTs. Each tenant mints one or more opaque bearer tokens; your IdP presents such a token on every /scim/v2/* call:

  • Minting requires lm_admin (normal user-JWT auth), and only for your own tenant — the {tenantId} in the path must match the caller's authenticated tenant, otherwise 403.
  • The plaintext token (lmscim_<43 url-safe chars>) is returned once at mint. Only its SHA-256 hash is stored; it is never logged and never shown again. Lose it → revoke and mint a new one.
  • On an inbound /scim/v2/* request, ScimAuthFilter hashes the presented bearer and looks it up. A match resolves the tenant and the issuer the token was minted for; all database work in that request then runs under that tenant's Row-Level Security policy. The regular JWT filter (TenantContextFilter) recognises the /scim/v2/* path and steps aside — SCIM is the only auth path for those routes. Missing, unknown, or revoked token → 401 with a SCIM-shaped error body.
  • A token is also scoped to one issuer: it can only see and touch users whose identity was keyed to that issuer. It cannot reach local users, another IdP's users, or another tenant's users — such lookups return a SCIM 404, not a leak.

Revocation is immediate: DELETE on the token sets revoked_at, and the very next lookup rejects it.

docs.title: Wiring your IdP
docs.text:
1. Mint a token (as an lm_admin of the tenant). The issuer must be the exact iss value of the JWTs your IdP sends to the hub — SCIM (idp_issuer) and JIT login (token iss) must key the same (idp_issuer, idp_subject) row, or SCIM will manage a parallel set of users that logins never hit.
curl -X POST "https://<hub>/api/tenants/<tid>/scim-tokens" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <your lm_admin JWT>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/acme", "label": "okta-prod"}'
# → 201 {"id":1,"issuer":"…","label":"okta-prod","token":"lmscim_…"}   ← save the token NOW
  1. Configure the IdP's SCIM provisioning app:
  2. Base URL: https://<hub>/scim/v2
  3. Authentication: OAuth Bearer Token (a.k.a. "HTTP Header" / "Bearer") with the lmscim_… value.

  4. Content type: application/scim+json (PATCH also accepts application/json).

  5. Map attributes: externalId must be the same value as the JWT subject claim (sub by default) — it is the join key. userName, displayName / name, and the primary emails entry are synced as profile data.

  6. Verify: most IdPs run a connectivity test against GET /scim/v2/ServiceProviderConfig (no auth surprises there — it declares patch and filter supported; bulk, sort, etag, and changePassword unsupported), then a dedup lookup like GET /scim/v2/Users?filter=userName eq "jdoe" before creating.

The end-to-end proof lives in the Helm smoke test (deploy/helm/up.sh, the "SCIM deprovisioning loop"): provision → login 200 → PATCH active:false → login 403.

docs.title: The /scim/v2/Users contract
docs.text:
Verb Path What it does POST /scim/v2/Users Find-or-create by (issuer, externalId), then apply active + profile from the body. 201 with the representation. Authoritative: a re-POST revives a soft-deleted user and may re-activate an archived one. externalId is required. GET /scim/v2/Users/{id} One user by lumnik id. 404 if absent, deleted, or keyed to a different issuer. GET /scim/v2/Users?filter=… Only externalId eq "x" and userName eq "x" (the dedup-before-create forms Okta/Entra use). Returns 0 or 1 result. Any other filter expression returns an empty list, not an error. Soft-deleted users are excluded; deactivated ones still appear (re-provisionable). PUT /scim/v2/Users/{id} Full replace: applies active, display name, and primary email from the body. PATCH /scim/v2/Users/{id} The deprovisioning operation: replace of the top-level active attribute only (path is case-insensitive). A non-boolean active, or any op other than replace targeting it, is rejected with 400 — a malformed value is never coerced into a deactivation. Operations on other paths are silently ignored. DELETE /scim/v2/Users/{id} Soft-delete, 204. The user drops out of SCIM listings; the row itself remains, keeping the (issuer, externalId) key occupied so a later login resolves to the deleted row and is refused — see GDPR & personal data.

Deactivate vs erase — what each does:

  • active: false archives the user — the operation your IdP should send on departure.
    • The row and its history stay intact: archived_at is stamped (and updated_at bumped, like any update); created_at never changes.
    • Denial is immediate, whatever the token's shape: the request filter checks the archived state on every call — a user_id-claim token (what the bundled realm emits) and an external (issuer, subject) identity are both refused with the same 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"}, still-valid token or not.
    • JIT never reactivates — only SCIM, being authoritative, can push the user back into service with active: true.
    • The SCIM write itself leaves no audit trail: an admin-driven archive lands in core.audit_event (identity.app_user is @Auditable), but a SCIM-driven write does not — the SCIM filter never sets the request context the audit listener reads, so it skips the very deprovisioning event an access reviewer most wants to see. See GDPR & personal data → the audit trail.
  • DELETE soft-deletes. It is reversible by a SCIM re-POST of the same (issuer, externalId); nothing hard-deletes the row automatically.
  • Neither is a GDPR erasure. No erase endpoint exists today — removing a soft-deleted row for good is an operator action, documented in GDPR & personal data.

docs.title: What is NOT supported
docs.text:
Deliberately scoped to deprovisioning; the hub does not pretend otherwise:

  • Groups — no /scim/v2/Groups resource. Roles are managed in the IdP realm (role management), not pushed over SCIM.
  • Bulk operations, sorting, etags, changePassword — declared unsupported in ServiceProviderConfig, and genuinely absent.
  • Pagination — no startIndex/count; the only list forms are the two eq filters above, which return at most one result.
  • The full SCIM PATCH path grammar — e.g. emails[type eq "work"].value is ignored. Full profile replacement goes through PUT.
  • /scim/v2/Schemas and /scim/v2/ResourceTypes — not implemented. IdPs that hard-require schema discovery need their attribute mappings configured by hand.
  • Unfiltered GET /scim/v2/Users returns an empty list, not the tenant's user population.

docs.title: Token lifecycle
docs.text:
All three endpoints require lm_admin and your own tenant id in the path:

# Mint — plaintext token in the response ONCE, never retrievable again
POST   /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens          {"issuer": "<idp iss>", "label": "okta-prod"}

# List active tokens — id, issuer, label, createdAt; never the hash, never the plaintext
GET    /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens

# Revoke — effective immediately, 204
DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens/{id}

Rotation is mint-then-revoke: mint the new token, switch the IdP over, revoke the old one. Several tokens can be active at once (use label to tell them apart), so rotation needs no provisioning outage.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Plain 404/no route on every /scim/v2/* call — not the SCIM-shaped error body above Running the open-source edition: the SCIM resource classes are excluded from that build (see the edition note at the top of this page). Deploy the default self-host/Helm build instead. 401 invalid SCIM token on /scim/v2/* Missing Authorization: Bearer header, a token that was never minted for this hub, or a revoked token. The response is identical in all three cases by design. 403 when minting/listing/revoking tokens Your JWT lacks lm_admin, or the {tenantId} in the path is not your own tenant (an lm_admin cannot manage another tenant's SCIM credentials). 404 on GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /scim/v2/Users/{id} No such user in this tenant, the user was soft-deleted, or the user's idp_issuer differs from the token's issuer — the most common wiring mistake. Check that the token's issuer equals the exact iss of your IdP's JWTs, byte for byte (scheme, host, port, path). IdP dedup search finds nothing, then POST returns an existing user Normal: the filter forms exclude soft-deleted rows, and POST is find-or-create — it revives/updates rather than duplicating. Deactivated user can still call the API A request already executing when the archive lands finishes; every request after it is denied at the filter, still-valid token or not. If later calls still succeed, verify the PATCH actually landed (GET /scim/v2/Users/{id} → "active": false), and that the issuer matches (see the 404 row).

docs.title: Relationship to JIT arrival
docs.text: Arrival and departure are two halves of one identity key. On first login through your IdP, JitUserProvisioner creates the lumnik user keyed on (idp_issuer, idp_subject); SCIM addresses the same row through (issuer, externalId). JIT is deliberately passive: it creates, but never reactivates or recreates — once SCIM (or an admin) has archived or deleted a user, only SCIM can bring them back. For the login side — brokered IdPs, issuer configuration, the subject claim — see BYO IdP.
